articles.content: A television drama no longer needs a television-sized screen, or even a half-hour episode. Microdramas — serialized stories filmed vertically and delivered in episodes often lasting a minute or two — are becoming a growing part of the streaming business. The format first took off in China , where producers condensed familiar soap opera plots — such as secret fortunes, time travel and long-awaited revenge — into episodes short enough to watch while waiting for a bus. The total amount of users of microdrama apps in China grew from 10 million to 400 million in three years . Microdrama platforms have developed a distinctive business model that sets them apart from traditional TV. Viewers can watch a handful of episodes before having to purchase virtual coins, subscribe or watch advertisements to unlock more. On DramaBox, for instance, viewers of Think Again! I’m the Hidden Boss Mom can watch the first 16 episodes free before paying for the remaining 36. Read more: TikTok’s popular microdramas shrink TV into bite-sized chunks The model has helped create a fast-growing industry . Microdramas generated US$11 billion worldwide in 2025 and are estimated to earn about US$14 billion in 2026. But the industry’s growth does not guarantee profitability. Industry and market research shows that while production costs are lower, attracting audiences is expensive, competition is intensifying and regulation remains unpredictable. How microdramas find their audiences Microdramas primarily rely on two distribution strategies . The first uses short teaser clips on TikTok or Instagram to attract viewers to dedicated apps, such as ReelShort and DramaBox, where they then pay to watch complete series. The second strategy involves distributing entire series through established video platforms, such as YouTube, where advertising revenue can support production. Microdramas generated more than 6.5 billion views on YouTube in the first half of 2026 . YouTube has also introduced the ability to group shorts into seasons and episodes , making serialized viewing easier within the platform. Other companies are trying to capitalize on existing audiences. In October, Tencent introduced Green Bubble, a free microdrama service integrated into its WeChat app. Users can discover series through search, links in a channel’s video feed or a section highlighting what their friends are watching. TikTok has also announced a partnership with a studio to produce microdramas . Its parent company, ByteDance, also operates Hongguo, a short-drama application that relies on algorithm-driven recommendations to attract viewers. How the business model works Microdrama platforms use several approaches to generate revenue. On DramaBox, viewers can subscribe, buy coins to unlock episodes or earn coins by watching ads . Green Bubble is free to watch and generates revenue through advertisements inserted into episodes. The payment structure is central to the format. Unlike a cinema ticket that provides access to an entire film or a streaming subscription that unlocks a catalogue, microdrama apps can charge viewers at particular moments in a story , often at cliffhangers when they are asked to pay to find out what happens next. This approach has raised consumer protection concerns. The consumer protection committee in the Chinese province of Jiangsu recorded 167,870 online complaints and other consumer-related reports concerning microdramas in the first half of 2024. Complaints included unclear charging and refund policies, misleading payment arrangements and difficulties cancelling subscriptions. Its investigation also found that some platforms did not clearly disclose the total cost of watching a series. Older consumers were particularly vulnerable to repeated purchases . Some companies are starting to use microdramas as advertising vehicles. American food company Bob Evans, for example, is releasing a 20-episode holiday series Christmas at Maple Hollow Inn through its own channels. Microdrama studio Pixie Studios integrates the company’s products into the story . High revenue doesn’t mean bigger profits Despite the market’s growth, the economic longevity of the industry remains an issue. Attracting viewers can be expensive, even when producing the shows themselves costs relatively little. FlexTV’s parent company, Mega Matrix, reported that advertising expenses accounted for 43 per cent of its total revenue in the first half of 2026 . Crazy Maple Studio, which runs ReelShort, nearly doubled its revenue in 2025 to 5.72 billion yuan, while its company-wide net loss was about 86 million yuan . Production costs are comparatively low. American streaming company Mansa produces microdramas on budgets from US$100,000 to US$250,000 per series . Low production costs allow producers to experiment with new ideas and take risks that would be difficult to justify with traditional TV budgets. But they also lower the barrier of entry for competitors, making it easier for rival studios to produce similar content. A Wall Street Journal segment about the microdrama boom. Artificial intelligence could push production costs down further. Kunlun Tech, which owns DramaWave, estimates it can make a microdrama series with AI for under US$20,000 , compared with $150,000 to $200,000 for a comparable series with human actors in dominant markets. AI-generated productions are already making an impact, with more than 94 per cent of new microdramas in China this year being AI-generated . At the end of October, 86 of the 100 titles on Hongguo’s trending chart were reportedly AI-made . As AI-generated content becomes more common, demand for some human performers and production workers will likely decline . What may strain the business model Hollywood studios and video platforms are feeling the pressure, and established streaming services and social platforms are increasingly adopting elements of the format. Omdia found that microdrama apps generate more daily viewing time than the biggest streaming platforms . Disney+ has added a vertical clip feed , HBO Max has begun testing one and YouTube now encourages creators to publish vertical series . Competition from established platforms could give microdramas access to larger audiences, but it also puts pressure on dedicated apps to differentiate their content and retain subscribers. Regulation is another area of uncertainty, particularly in China. China’s broadcast regulator recently launched a two-month campaign targeting eight types of content, including violent, sexually suggestive and wealth-flaunting material . Platform content moderation is also being tested, as Hongguo faces a lawsuit over the alleged unauthorized use of actress Zhao Liying’s likeness in AI-generated microdramas . Other alleged victims have said they are preparing legal action , so more disputes may follow. Recent Chinese regulations on microdramas require platforms offering paid content to clearly disclose pricing information and prohibit the use of algorithms designed to encourage addictive behaviour or excessive spending. In the United States, California requires businesses to obtain express consent to automatic renewal and lets customers who sign up online cancel online . Though a cliffhanger can get someone to watch one more episode, the hard test will always come in the end. Will viewers open the app again on their own, or will the company have to place an advertisement to reach them again? articles.content: Recently, starting in August, poet and author Nayyirah Waheed began posting a series of images to Instagram that reignited existing debates within Instagram poetry. In her post, Waheed said Rupi Kaur’s bestselling book of poetry, milk and honey (2014), “extracted” the style, form and ideas of her 2013 self-published collection, salt . The author, based in the United States, also said that Andrews McMeel Publishing worked to erase Waheed from the narrative of Instapoetry, calling their actions “corporate gaslighting” and “hostile takeover attempts.” In 2018, Vice asked Kaur how she deals with accusations of plagiarism in general and those specifically by Waheed. She said that many other artists are looking at similar subjects and “me using a couple of words that the other person also uses, doesn’t equal plagiarism.” . One of the long-standing questions raised in this debate is who is the originator of Instapoetry? Did Kaur “extract” from Waheed as she says? And why did Kaur became the genre’s public face? The allegations of plagiarism from Waheed as well as her characterization of this process as anti-Black erasure are serious and warrant careful attention. Some reporters have also argued that the praise of Kaur’s poetry over Waheed’s is rooted in anti-Blackness . Waheed’s posts also make a broader challenge: that salt. didn’t just precede milk and honey , but established the visual and formal language later recognized as Instapoetry. Waheed self-published salt. in 2013 after gaining popularity on Twitter and Instagram, then self-published nemja in 2014. Kaur is considered one of the first and most successful Instapoets and has by and large become representative of the genre. Instapoetry is a genre of poetry that circulates on Instagram and often features short, free-verse lines, limited punctuation and line drawings. The poetry typically favours emotional directness, brevity and formal constraints, including lower-case typography and minimal punctuation . As a researcher studying women’s writing and publishing infrastructures, I argue that genres are formed through complex relations among communities, influences, audiences and platforms. Literary history often relies on the idea of one great individual who single-handedly creates a genre. But genres usually grow out of many writers, readers, influences and communities over time . Rupi Kaur, the face of Instapoetry Canadian poet Rupi Kaur, who also identifies as Punjabi Sikh, is arguably one of the most commercially successful Instapoets. Her poetry is often written in lower-case letters and sparingly includes punctuation. She says the style is one way to break English rules but it also reflects some of her heritage and the Gurmukhi script, which has no uppercase. . Kaur currently has more than four million followers on Instagram and has sold over 12 million books worldwide. She has said Instagram allowed her to sidestep gatekeepers to the publishing industry who were “never going to pay attention to (her) anyway.” Kaur’s success sparked heated debate in traditional poetry communities, with some arguing that Instagram democratized poetry by allowing previously marginalized writers to sidestep gatekeepers and publish outside traditional structures . Others, like British poet Rebecca Watts, characterize Instapoetry as “artless,” lament that poetry has not escaped “social media’s dumbing effect” and call Instapoetry a “huckster’s paradise.” Read more: Instapoetry is successful and there’s nothing wrong with that The ‘blueprint’ of a genre? Kaur self-published milk and honey in 2014. After Instagram censored her menstruation photographs , Kaur went viral and signed with Andrews McMeel Publishing who republished milk and honey to wide commercial success. In 2017, Rolling Stone dubbed her the “Queen of the Instapoets.” That same year, BookNet Canada named Kaur as a driving force behind increased poetry sales . In one of her September Instagram posts, Waheed says: “@rupikaur you took credit for my blueprint,” challenging the industry’s elevation of Kaur as the singular face of Instapoetry. By doing this, Waheed suggests that one person can be responsible for the founding of a literary style and history. But can any one writer supply the “blueprint” for an entire genre? Instapoetry’s influences As U.S.-based literary theorist Carolyn Miller explains in her foundational study on genre , genres are not formal categories but emerge through the ways we encounter, interpret, use and reproduce texts. Some of the text and style features Waheed says originated with her 2013 work, salt. , were not developed in isolation. They belong to a wider ecology of online writing and reading already taking shape across social media platforms throughout the 2000s-2010s, as I have argued in my PhD thesis. Several specific digital locations of this era can be seen as key influences to the later development of Instapoetry. From this perspective, lower-case typography, brevity, white space, illustration and emotional directness are formal conventions, not a genre in themselves. Tumblr, for example, was a particularly significant site of poetic experimentation for writers at this time. Its multimedia interface encouraged combinations of text, photographs, GIFs, drawings and handwritten fragments. Poetry circulated through tags such as #poetry, #poetsoftumblr and #spilledink, creating a participatory culture of reposting, remixing and response. Minimalist typography, including lower-case letters and sparse punctuation, was widespread on Tumblr as an internet vernacular rather than one writer’s signature. Digital spoken word communities, largely rooted in North American Black culture , also influenced the Instapoetry genre . By the 2010s, YouTube channels like Button Poetry had brought live poetry to large online audiences. These works favoured direct address, emotional intensity and accessible language, and often addressed gender, race, migration and trauma — themes that would become central to Instapoetry . Canadian Instapoets, including Kaur, were on Tumblr, performing at open mic nights in Toronto , Surrey and Delta, B.C. and watching slam performances on YouTube. These poets encountered — and were shaped by — poetry circulating through Tumblr, live readings and viral videos. The Instagram platform also played a critical role in developing the genre . The social media app was the first to focus predominantly on the visual , with images taking centre-stage and text — in the form of captions, comments and hashtags — framing the image. Instapoetry emerged through many writers, esthetics, technologies and audiences moving across platforms and between digital and in-person spaces. It became recognizable through self-publication, networked circulation, audience interaction, algorithms, performance, print and literary entrepreneurship. The genre can therefore be understood as something produced and continually negotiated by poets, readers, publishers, critics and platforms. Waheed has an important place in the genre’s history, but even an innovative writer cannot alone create a genre. Where do we go from here? Waheed’s recent posts reminds us that literary history is never neutral: it is shaped by who is remembered, who is marketed and whose innovations are made visible. Her allegations of the “extraction” of her work and her analysis that this is part of a continuum of anti-Black erasure require attention, particularly in an industry with long histories of marginalizing Black women writers. Waheed is an important and under-recognized figure in the genre, but Instapoetry has no sole architect. The history of Instapoetry is best understood as a story with more than one originator. It’s a history of overlapping influence, platform-specific experimentation, performance, readership and commercial power. The question then may be less “who owns Instapoetry?” than who’s been permitted to represent it — and who has profited from that representation. articles.content: Carrie-Anne Moss in Crave's _YAGA_. The series, based on the play of the same name, draws on Baba Yaga from East European folklore. (Crave/Christopher Lawrence) Baba Yaga is a terrifying witch from eastern European folklore , found in folktales from Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and other Slavic countries. Yet she is more than just a scary monster. In many folktales, she offers advice and assistance to characters who are kind and clever, while punishing rude, selfish ones. Baba Yaga’s intriguing duality — her ability to be both a villain and a saviour, a figure of destruction and renewal, of darkness and light — has inspired artists and writers to produce lively adaptations that have travelled well beyond eastern European folklore and made her a favourite among audiences worldwide. The recent Crave series YAGA , starring Carrie-Anne Moss and Hudson Williams, is the latest in a long history of versions of her tales . The series, whose showrunner wrote the acclaimed play of the same name , imagines “ the myth of Baba Yaga as a contemporary mystery thriller .” As an anthropologist who has studied folklore and witchcraft, I want to examine the original Baba Yaga and how she has been received by western audiences. Trailer for ‘Yaga,’ starring Carrie-Anne Moss and Hudson Williams. Deep in a forest In folktales, Baba Yaga lives deep in the forest in a round house that spins on chicken feet, surrounded by a fence made from the bones and skulls of her victims — a grim warning of her cannibalistic nature to anyone who would dare intrude on her. She flies through the skies in a giant mortar and pestle, making a dreadful noise as she crushes her victim’s bones. articles.content: Tokyo then, St. John's now? A giant squid attacks a bait squid off the coast of Tokyo in 2006. (Tsunemi Kubodera/National Science Museum of Japan) , CC BY When I learned that Netflix planned to film the miniseries Below , about a sea monster terrorizing a Newfoundland outport , I thought to myself: “THIS I’ve gotta see!” First, the series showcases coastal Newfoundland, where I was raised and live. Second, I have studied ocean life in the island’s waters for most of my career. Third, it features the marine lab where I work , the Oceans Sciences Centre. And fourth, it stars a giant squid(-ish) animal (sorry Josh Hartnett). Giant squid have a special place in Newfoundland folklore and science, from early encounters with fishermen to some of the first scientific evidence of their existence. Unveiling the giant squid One key player in this history was the Irish clergyman Moses Harvey , who moved to Newfoundland in 1852 and undertook natural history research in what was then a British colony. Harvey’s research included revealing the existence of giant squid to the world based on a specimen that washed ashore. Fishermen had brought it to him to photograph and communicate to the science community in London. Arms, tentacles and head (buccal region, including beak visible) of a giant squid from Logy Bay, Newfoundland, photographed draped over Moses Harvey’s sponge bath in November 1873. (Variously attributed to John Maunder, Moses Harvey and Messrs. McKenny and Parsons) Fast forward to the 1960s, when the founding director of the Ocean Sciences Centre, Fred Aldrich , joined the faculty at Memorial University and soon focused his career on pursuing giant squid. Although Aldrich tried to catch a living specimen, he only obtained squid that washed up on beaches. Newfoundland is one of the global hotspots where giant squid appear more frequently, every 30 years or so (New Zealand is another, attesting to giant squid affinity for cooler waters). Below ‘s arrival roughly coincides with one of those cycles. The Rooms provincial museum in St. John’s displays a preserved version of one of these amazing animals. Giant squid: Not known to be vindictive Early in the series, we meet an (oddly) barefooted marine biologist walking through the hallways of the marine lab. This scene earned a loud “ewww” from my graduate students on the grounds of hygiene as well as occupational health and safety. The biologist turns out to be the expert on giant squid and the voice of sanity when fishermen, the military and a local developer all pursue the creature (nicknamed “Mudder” by the locals, foreshadowing why she is attacking the community) with bloodlust. This marine biologist also provides impromptu medical expertise when residents fall ill from drinking ice water tainted by the animal. (Side note, DO NOT entrust your local marine biologist with urgent medical needs — we are not that type of doctor!) I could join the Facebook crowd quibbling about who got the Newfoundland accents right and who missed the mark. Or I could ask why the Coast Guard would fully abandon people living on a small, isolated island in crisis. But Below generally did a good job on the science. The biology of the animal was reasonably plausible, including its swimming skills and even its ability to survive in ice. As a (likely necessary) stretch, I thought the intellectual prowess and directed vindictiveness of the squid in the series pushed the limits of credibility, although researchers have documented some impressive abilities in cephalopods (of which giant squid are members). Still, it was a good effort to maintain scientific plausibility and fun to see marine biota as the star attraction. Historical accuracy I took a course in marine invertebrates from Aldrich when I was an undergraduate in the early 1980s. Although he was in the late stages of his career, his enthusiasm for giant squid was still evident in his lectures. He would have loved to have seen the first live footage of giant squid in the wild collected just 20 years ago by Japanese scientists, and I think he would have enjoyed watching Below and he’d be happy I’m writing about it. I certainly enjoyed watching Below , not just because of the Newfoundland setting but because it seemed entirely appropriate for the story, which was in some ways a homage to Newfoundland and its ocean history. The plot weaved in the innate capacity of local fishers to adapt and work together to solve challenges (who can “put the arse back in a cat,” as locals would say). It addressed the collapse of the northern cod fishery that threw some 37,000 Newfoundlanders out of work. And it began with a striking scene about the government’s resettlement of more than 28,000 residents of many small coastal communities to larger centres in the 1950s and '60s. It also captured the general mistrust of government in outport communities. My CFA (come from away) graduate students also appreciated seeing the “Screeching In” ceremony , and the real sense of Newfoundland conveyed by the series. Read more: The trauma caused by resettlement in Newfoundland and Labrador must be acknowledged Stoking interest in the ocean I am not a particular fan of the horror genre, though I recognize its nod to productions from decades earlier when creatures emerged from the ocean depths to wreak havoc on an unsuspecting humanity (think Godzilla , Jaws , and Orca ). Though the genre isn’t for everyone, most people I asked said they enjoyed the series, and particularly the Newfoundland ambience. I also applaud the Below team for communicating the complexity of the ocean, and their efforts to capture the imagination and interest of the public with its many unknowns. The series also underscored the ongoing potential for ocean exploration. Scientists discover thousands of new marine species every year and could discover many more if there were more of us. Many of these discoveries come from the deep sea , where giant squid spend most of their time. Most new marine species are small animals, but, as scientists sample more ocean, a surprise discovery occasionally emerges not unlike the giant squid in Below . Perhaps given Below ’s success ( the No. 1 ranked show in Canada on Netflix the week after its release , with an 87 per cent Tomatometer on Rotten Tomatoes ), Hollywood might see some potential in telling exciting stories that bring the ocean into our living rooms. That focus could inspire a new generation of scientists. I can’t help thinking that watching Jaws and Orca when I was an impressionable teen helped to push my career interests towards the ocean, where my ancestors had also earned their living. articles.content: Elizabeth Holmes is questioned by Nathan Fielder in 'You Can See Everything.' (A24) This story contains a spoiler about ‘You Can See Everything .’ Canadian comedian Nathan Fielder’s runaway-hit documentary You Can See Everything reintroduces audiences to Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes, who was convicted of fraud in 2022 . Holmes maintains she is innocent . Through Fielder’s lens, the film prompts us to question her conduct anew by exploring the meaning of acting, drama, truth, lies and fiction. In the film, Holmes objects to a quote of hers reported by the New York Times . According to the Times , Holmes said of actors portraying her: “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” In Fielder’s documentary, Holmes’s husband reads the quote and says it doesn’t sound like something she would say . He suggests Holmes said instead: “They’re playing a character they created,” and she agrees. Partly through the film’s interviews with Holmes and her husband, as well as commentary by Fielder, viewers are led to wonder: Has she been playing a character she created, intended to deceive others? Is she now playing a role? Does she even know? Playing a role If Holmes is deliberately playing a role, we are inclined to condemn her as a fraudulent deceiver, well-deserving of her punishment; if not, we may be more inclined to see her sympathetically — flawed, caught up in a scheme largely wrought by others. ‘You Can See Everything’ trailer. It might seem that, because each person knows what they’re doing, they’re the authority on whether they are playing a role. But Fielder’s film, and his previous work that straddles the line between awkward comedy and social inquiry , challenges where the boundaries lie. In his HBO docuseries The Rehearsal , Fielder plays himself as a director helping people prepare for difficult situations by staging elaborate rehearsals of how they might unfold . The series leads the audience to question the relationship between the rehearsals and the real situation they mean to influence. Actions, imitations One way to think about this is by examining the difference between doing things and acting as though we’re doing them — for the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle, the difference between an action and an imitation. To frame this issue more carefully, we can turn to a distinction Aristotle drew between “action” and “production.” For Aristotle, the arts are particular kinds of know-how. A shoemaker, for instance, knows how to produce shoes. Drama, writes Aristotle, knows how to produce the imitation ( mimēsis ) of actions . The actor’s aim is to produce a compelling imitation of someone, say, making a shoe. That imitated action is the product of the art. When done well, the audience is convinced they have seen someone do the action, perhaps briefly forgetting it was only an imitation. Often, an actor playing a shoemaker does not go so far as to make a shoe. But what if they do? ‘The Fielder Method’ The fourth episode of The Rehearsal , “The Fielder Method,” sees Fielder describe a method to train people to perform on his show. Fielder invites actors to shadow a person, called their “primary,” to learn how to imitate them in the rehearsals. He goes so far as to have them work the job of their primary or even move into a similar living arrangement. Following this method, it very well may be the case that an actor playing a shoemaker makes a real shoe. “The Fielder Method” shows that the distinction between “imitated action” and “genuine action” is porous. An audience, actor can get lost An effective imitation convinces audiences, temporarily, that we are witnessing the action, and we respond to it, at least in part, as a doing of that action. The audience can get lost in whether what they are seeing is an action or its imitation. An effective imitation, then, can be a powerful tool in the hands of someone intent on deception. Yet, as Fielder’s work also suggests, the actor can get caught up in their role. In The Rehearsal (“Pretend Daddy”), Fielder (playing himself) is rehearsing parenting a six-year old child. The child actor playing his child becomes attached to Fielder, calling him “daddy.” Fielder himself seemingly has real feelings for the child actor. If what an actor does as an imitation coincides with the actual deed so precisely that its outcome is indistinguishable from the real thing, its status hangs on what comes next: The actor’s stepping out of character and returning to “real life.” But what if the actor doesn’t step out of character? What if they leave “real life” behind? In The Rehearsal , Fielder becomes so committed to understanding pilots that he becomes one, flying a Boeing 737 from takeoff to landing. Is it plausible that Holmes, too, began intent on deception, playing a brilliant, Steve Jobs-like CEO, but then became lost in the role, increasingly unable to acknowledge distance between herself and the character she created? Or is this explanation a perfect hiding place to deny responsibility? ‘Why would I deceive you?’ A viral scene where Holmes asks Fielder, “Why would I deceive you?” is astonishing because there is such a clear reason for Holmes to deceive Fielder. In the film, partly through Fielder’s dialogue with actor Amanda Seyfried , who played Holmes in a miniseries , the film deals with how to understand Holmes. Their dialogue is interspersed with newly created scenes of Seyfried playing Holmes in Fielder’s documentary to study her, using the technique developed in The Rehearsal . One explanation could be that Holmes believes herself, or has become lost in her role. This would not excuse her crimes. But it might suggest that understanding her properly requires us to think about the role of imitation and art in our lives, just as Fielder’s works challenge us to do. On the other hand, what exactly have we seen? Commentators have raised ethical concerns around how Fielder’s relationship to his subject shapes what we do and importantly don’t see (such as the impacts of Holmes’s fraud) — or genre questions , including whether it really should be called a documentary. Read more: Can you see everything? Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes face off in You Can See Everything A compelling imitation, Aristotle tells us , is delightful because we love to learn, and imitation teaches us. This may be why scores of audiences are going to cinemas to watch an almost three-hour-long documentary . Drama can be deployed for deception, but as both Aristotle and Fielder show us, it can also be an essential vehicle for questioning our assumptions about reality. Fielder invites actors to shadow a person, called their “primary,” to learn how to imitate them in the rehearsals. He goes so far as to have them work the job of their primary or even move into a similar living arrangement. Following this method, it very well may be the case that an actor playing a shoemaker makes a real shoe. “The Fielder Method” shows that the distinction between “imitated action” and “genuine action” is porous. An audience, actor can get lost An effective imitation convinces audiences, temporarily, that we are witnessing the action, and we respond to it, at least in part, as a doing of that action. The audience can get lost in whether what they are seeing is an action or its imitation. An effective imitation, then, can be a powerful tool in the hands of someone intent on deception. Yet, as Fielder’s work also suggests, the actor can get caught up in their role. In The Rehearsal (“Pretend Daddy”), Fielder (playing himself) is rehearsing parenting a six-year old child. The child actor playing his child becomes attached to Fielder, calling him “daddy.” Fielder himself seemingly has real feelings for the child actor. If what an actor does as an imitation coincides with the actual deed so precisely that its outcome is indistinguishable from the real thing, its status hangs on what comes next: The actor’s stepping out of character and returning to “real life.” But what if the actor doesn’t step out of character? What if they leave “real life” behind? In The Rehearsal , Fielder becomes so committed to understanding pilots that he becomes one, flying a Boeing 737 from takeoff to landing. Is it plausible that Holmes, too, began intent on deception, playing a brilliant, Steve Jobs-like CEO, but then became lost in the role, increasingly unable to acknowledge distance between herself and the character she created? Or is this explanation a perfect hiding place to deny responsibility? ‘Why would I deceive you?’ A viral scene where Holmes asks Fielder, “Why would I deceive you?” is astonishing because there is such a clear reason for Holmes to deceive Fielder. In the film, partly through Fielder’s dialogue with actor Amanda Seyfried , who played Holmes in a miniseries , the film deals with how to understand Holmes. Their dialogue is interspersed with newly created scenes of Seyfried playing Holmes in Fielder’s documentary to study her, using the technique developed in The Rehearsal . One explanation could be that Holmes believes herself, or has become lost in her role. This would not excuse her crimes. But it might suggest that understanding her properly requires us to think about the role of imitation and art in our lives, just as Fielder’s works challenge us to do. On the other hand, what exactly have we seen? Commentators have raised ethical concerns around how Fielder’s relationship to his subject shapes what we do and importantly don’t see (such as the impacts of Holmes’s fraud) — or genre questions , including whether it really should be called a documentary. Read more: Can you see everything? Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes face off in You Can See Everything A compelling imitation, Aristotle tells us , is delightful because we love to learn, and imitation teaches us. This may be why scores of audiences are going to cinemas to watch an almost three-hour-long documentary . Drama can be deployed for deception, but as both Aristotle and Fielder show us, it can also be an essential vehicle for questioning our assumptions about reality. The Canadian poet, novelist and singer-songwriter died Nov. 7, 2016, just one day before United States President Donald Trump was first elected . Ten years later, as the Democrat “blue wave” hopes to close the bracket on a president who once memed himself as Jesus personified , Cohen’s legacy has become effortlessly epic — even biblical — in quite a different way. Tribute gatherings Tribute gatherings for the singer abound. Cohen was the subject of a sold-out event at the Toronto International Festival of Authors at the end of October. Adam Cohen’s family tour, which began in Canada this month and reaches Europe in winter 2027, pairs his father’s music with archival photos and film . Ottawa’s Gladstone Theatre advertised their “Ten Years Gone” commemoration with a question quite suggestive to people like me who study the evolution of sacred texts: “What would Cohen say today?” Cohen’s ‘contemporary psalms’ As an answer, I highlight an under-celebrated part of Cohen’s poetry and song. As I detail in my 2023 book Prophets of Love: The Unlikely Kinship of Leonard Cohen and the Apostle Paul , all of Cohen’s work is infused with biblical allusions. But some of Cohen’s work does more than echo biblical themes. It takes on biblical format, in the tradition of poetic prayer known in Hebrew as tehillim . Tehillim, or Psalms, inform the Jewish liturgical tradition of addressing God directly, not only in praise, but also in lament, desperation and challenge . This is most explicit in what publisher McClelland and Stewart called Cohen’s “contemporary psalms” in his Book of Mercy . In 1984, as Cohen turned 50, his life provided the material for the 50 psalms of lament, complaint, joy, doubt, adoration and desperation that made up this poetry collection. Like the biblical Psalms, these short poems are numbered rather than titled. Cohen described the collection as “meant for people like myself who could use it, at a particular time,” as “a book of prayer.” Many interpreters continue to analyze this collection as Tehillim . Writing liturgy Although modest about himself in public, Cohen never lacked ambition for his poetry. Rabbi Mordecai Finley , who has read Cohen’s poems aloud for High Holy Days, recalls Cohen confiding that he felt he was always writing not just poetry, but liturgy. Ben Sales points out that Cohen’s song “If It Be Your Will” echoes the Friday evening prayer service welcoming Shabbat, and “Who By Fire” is a nearly word-for-word arrangement of the High Holiday prayer, the “Unetaneh Tokef .” Cohen’s “ Anthem ,” with its famous line “that’s how the light gets in,” inspires ponderings from both Christians and Jews . And “ Hallelujah ,” — a biblical term heard in church services — is a star example of a Cohen song as religious anthem, despite its references to surprisingly carnal biblical texts . I believe Cohen’s grappling with the divine, whether overt, or nestled within his sensual poetry, might prove to be his most enduring memorial. Multiple traditions and levels Cohen biographer and author Harry Freedman reports that Cohen studied in India, referenced the Kabbalah frequently and knew the lore of the Christian Desert Mothers and Fathers . Both Kabbalah and early Christian ascetics blur the boundaries between the erotic and the divine. Cohen’s way of addressing the sensual and the spiritual simultaneously allows the same song to reach different people — or reach the same person at different times. He could also speak from multiple traditions. Cohen was an ordained Rinzai Zen monk , the grandson of a famous rabbi and Talmud scholar. As an impressionable child he went to mass with his Irish nanny in Montréal, a city of churches. In I’m Your Man , music journalist Sylvie Simmons chronicles how Cohen was a deeply knowledgeable Jew who moved comfortably between the Torah, Talmud, Tao Te Ching, Sufi mysticism and the New Testament. No religious tourist Fewer Canadians remember the literary critic Northrop Frye than know Cohen. But the poet turned out to be the perfect example of the professor’s point: the educated imagination lives and breathes the vocabulary of the sacred. Cohen was no religious tourist. Rather, the singer “spoke multiple religions” fluently, always from his Jewish roots. At this 10th yahrzeit of his passing, it’s worth considering to whom (besides his audiences) he addressed his final performances. In “Traveling Light,” from You Want it Darker , he sang: “But if the road leads back to you, Must I forget the things I knew …Traveling light, like we used to do.” Grappling with God Like the ultimate Psalmist, King David, dethroned and on the run , Cohen was at a low point in his career when he wrote Book of Mercy . In those dark days of seeming failure, before Jennifer Warnes’s Famous Blue Raincoat revived his career, Book of Mercy was the middle-aged Jewish poet’s attempt to leave at least something of permanence: “We talk in this manner, we sing the time-honoured songs, and we compose new ones, as we were commanded,” he wrote in “25.” Yet, for me, it is Cohen’s final albums 20 and 30 years later, as his life neared its end, that most resemble the Psalms in how they grapple with God. Psalms for every human experience Through the years, Cohen addressed God right before our eyes in the person of a lover. At the end of his life, he boldly exposed the relationship that had been there all along — perhaps most notably in the song “You Want it Darker.” Here, he addressed God as “My lord,” incorporated elements of the Jewish mourners’ prayer and adapted Rosh Hashanah liturgy . Was Cohen writing and adapting Kaddish for his own impending death? I believe so, although in true Cohen fashion his words also mourn humanity overall, and challenge the divine. Leonard Cohen’s ‘You Want it Darker.’ As I wrote in Prophets of Love , for Leonard as “Cohen” (Hebrew for priest), existential longing and divine connection are inseparably linked at the base of the human condition. So, 10 years later, even if you are already a devotee, have a listen again. Pay special attention to how Cohen challenges, pleads with, chastises and even woos the divine. If you are not yet a fan, buy one of the iconic Canadian’s final albums, when he could feel death waiting at the door . You may find that, just as for many faithful opening the ancient psalms, there’s material in Cohen’s contemporary psalms for every human experience, including yours. articles.content: For some, the lesson in needing to look presentable to society began with a reprimand about scuffed shoes. For others, it was a warning about stray hairs, an untidy hairline, trousers that needed pressing or a last-minute stain. A parent was often ready to send you back to the mirror, unwilling to let you leave looking as though nobody at home had taken the time to care for you. Behind these admonitions was an uneasy mixture of affection and discipline. Taking pride in one’s appearance communicated dignity , but it also reflected the demands of respectability in a world where Black people have often worked exceptionally hard for recognition routinely afforded to others. No one needed to grow up attending church to appreciate the ethic of “ Sunday Best .” Rooted in traditions of dressing for worship, the practice reflects a collective belief that appearance can express reverence for an occasion and regard for those with whom we share it. ‘Sunday Best’ exhibition at the AGO At the opening of the Art Gallery of Ontario’s “Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style,” the crowd understood the assignment. Attendees arrived dressed to impress, bringing sartorial flair to the celebration. Conceived and curated by a transnational team, including AGO curator Julie Crooks and fashion historian Jason Cyrus, with Amanda Bock and Clare Sauro , “Sunday Best” brings together garments, photographs and personal effects spanning Black diasporic life from the 1880s to the present. Displays of church fashion recall generations of Black women and the splendour of dress for Sunday worship. Elsewhere, the distinctive uniforms of the Black Panther Party are on display, a nod to the role clothing and fashion play in political organizing. The exhibition also honours Black dandies , alongside those who have challenged conventions of gender through the way they dress. Among them are Toronto-based trans soul singer Jackie Shane and the late fashion icon André Leon Talley, a long-time editor at Vogue magazine , whose styles helped to expand the possibilities of Black self-presentation. The exhibition also contains references to ballroom culture that show how Black traditions of dress and performance have been inherited and reimagined for self-expression and communal recognition. Renewed attention on Black fashion The exhibition traces how Black styles and cultural practices travel through migration. Visitors may recognize traces of traditions from their own families. A hat may evoke an auntie preparing for church, a family photograph the sober pride of relatives posing for a formal portrait . The curators bring these expressions of Black life together, drawing connections between diverse traditions. The exhibition arrives amid renewed public attention to Black fashion. Last year, New York’s Met Gala put Black dandyism on the global stage with its theme, “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style.” “Sunday Best” contributes to this conversation by showcasing the communal rituals that give style meaning. The exhibition calls attention to the pressures under which Black people have fashioned themselves. Respectability and beauty In an iconic 1956 photograph, Gordon Parks depicts Joanne Thornton Wilson and her niece Shirley Anne Kirksey standing beneath a neon “Colored Entrance” sign outside a department store, in Mobile, Alabama . Their elegant and dignified dress contrasts with the indignity of segregation. For generations, dressing well could be understood as a defence against racial scrutiny or a means of improving one’s social standing . But no degree of sartorial excellence could guarantee protection from discrimination. The demands of respectability also placed constraints on those whose expressions of gender or sexuality challenged accepted conventions. Covers of Ebony magazine on display offer another perspective. As a Black-led publication, Ebony helped cultivate images of Black beauty and achievement in the United States that spoke to how Black communities understood themselves, free from the stereotypes and expectations of mainstream audiences. Across these histories, the attention given to one’s appearance carried meanings beyond the judgments of others. Dressing for worship could express reverence, just as a carefully chosen outfit might bring pleasure or communicate regard for others. The Sunday best tradition thus emerges as an ethic of dignity and care, fostered within Black communities even when those qualities went unrecognized by the wider society. Black queerness The exhibition’s treatment of Black queerness unsettles the presumed divide between church traditions and ballroom culture. Black churches have held complicated relationships with queer people , offering spaces for artistic expression alongside experiences of exclusion. Through these church communities, Black queer people have inherited styles and sensibilities they continue to reinvent. Consider drag performer Kennedy Davenport’s viral appearance on The Pit Stop . Reacting to another queen’s outfit, she sang: “Black stockings, white shoes, shouldn’t be allowed in the church.” Her playful critique drew on the rules of Black church fashion, finding humour in a set of esthetic rules passed down through generations. Black queer performers have also helped shape gospel music and traditions of Black religious life , including in spaces where their sexuality was not fully accepted. In “Sunday Best,” the proximity of church fashion to ballroom culture highlights how these traditions inform one another. Through inventive clothing and performance, ballroom turns resourcefulness into glamour, creating spaces where beauty and ambition earn recognition. Read more: Black style and resistance: The Met Gala, dandyism and blackface in Canada A ‘habit of care’ In the exhibition, everyday grooming tools share space with dresses and photographs. Hairbrushes evoke the private rituals behind a public appearance. Many of these belongings have survived for decades. In her book Ordinary Notes , writer and scholar Christina Sharpe describes regard as “a habit of care.” She says: “It is appreciation and esteem. It is the right of repair.” Her words invite us to consider the attention given to these belongings and the lives they represent. The curators extend this ethic of care to bring these histories together. From garments and paintings to archival photographs and moving images, their staging treats Black cultural expression as worthy of preservation and public appreciation. Behind the displays lies the painstaking labour of conservation, ensuring these materials will encountered by new generations. Black artists have long struggled for recognition in Canadian institutions, giving moments like these added weight. In 2019, the AGO hosted “The Feast” , marking 30 years since the groundbreaking exhibition “Black Wimmin: When and Where We Enter.” The gathering brought 100 Black women and gender-nonconforming artists and cultural workers into AGO’s Walker Court. At the opening of “Sunday Best,” the carefully dressed crowd offered another expression of this cultural legacy. Across the gallery, objects once worn with pride had been kept with care, their stories deserving of the same attention. Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style is on view at the Art Gallery of Ontario until Feb. 28, 2027. articles.content: The appeal of leading man Edward Ferrars, played by George MacKay, is ramped up in this version. (Focus Features) Director Georgia Oakley’s new, unfettered Sense and Sensibility delivers a contemporary take on Jane Austen’s first published novel. At the beginning of the book, Henry Dashwood’s death leaves his grieving wife and three daughters ousted from their home. Norland Park is inherited by the son of a prior marriage, John, while the Dashwood women relocate to a small cottage in another county. The novel focuses on the two eldest daughters, Elinor and Marianne (in Oakley’s adaptation, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles) and their contrasting philosophies of sense and sensibility. Oakley has said she was inspired by Austen’s emphasis on sisterhood, and some reviews have noted the film’s strong depiction of this . The director has spoken to her interpretation of Austen as a writer who “was taking what she knew to be a commercial form … the romance framework,” while including “subversive” content . The film seeks to translate Austen’s 1811 feminism to a modern audience, but, for me as an Austen scholar, some important things are lost. Bold women who revel in nature We expect Austen heroines to take long walks in the English countryside , but this adaptation, more than any before, firmly plants its women in nature. The film is beautiful to watch: In the opening sequence, Marianne reclines on the ground amid tall reeds and contemplates a caterpillar balancing on her fingertip. Later, we see her bathing her feet in a cold brook; Elinor skips stones with her love interest. This is Jane Austen, unbuttoned. Both heroines wave aside social decorum when needed. Oakley’s Elinor even makes the first move. Once Edward Ferrars is a free man, she boldly kisses him on the lips with a windswept landscape as background. In conversation with other adaptations Oakley’s adaptation stands in conversation with previous versions. As literary critic Linda Hutcheon argues, earlier adaptations may “ be just as important as contexts … as any ‘original .’” Oakley draws on Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation in some ways, including in the depiction of leading men. Austen’s Edward Ferrars and Colonel Brandon may be underwhelming romantic interests. But their failure to capture the readers’ imagination is part of the point. While Oakley does highlight the women’s relationships anchoring Austen’s novel, she presents the male suitors more favourably — and this undermines Austen’s subversion of the romance plot. Literary scholar Deborah Kaplan has argued that the 1995 Sense and Sensibility and the 1996 Emma “harlequinize” Austen’s novels. We might say the same is true, to some extent, of Oakley’s version. Trailer for ‘Sense and Sensibility.’ Fulfilment in romance? Lee’s 1995 Sense and Sensibility cast Hugh Grant and Alan Rickman, setting up their respective characters, Edward Ferrars and Colonel Brandon, as romantic leads. Oakley’s men in these roles, George MacKay and Herbert Nordrum, don’t (yet) have the same Hollywood star power. But they follow in Grant and Rickman’s footsteps in romantic appeal. The film suggests both heroines find fulfilment in the courtship plot that Austen interrogates. For example, Oakley’s Edward, like Lee’s, endears himself to the audience by playfully entertaining the 13-year-old Margaret. Such scenes don’t exist in the novel. Oakley further ramps up Edward’s merit. In Austen, it’s not a mark in his favour that he fell in love with Lucy Steele and formed a secret engagement. In Oakley’s film, the alliance was arranged. Once the Steeles lose their fortune, he is expected to dissolve the engagement, but Edward is a man of honour. Treatment of Brandon, Willoughby Oakley’s Colonel Brandon, like Lee’s, is set up as a romantic hero. articles.content: Officials are meeting this week for the 21st Canada-European Union Leaders’ summit . It comes only a month after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered Canada associate membership . A draft statement from Montréal , where Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, von der Leyen and EU Council President António Costa met for two days to discuss strengthening ties, calls for an “ever closer association” that will result “in a more active foreign and security policy partnership.” The talks follow a series of milestones in the relationship between the transatlantic partners, including the announcement in July that Canada was joining the Eurovision song contest. It’s the first country to do so since Australia entered in 2015. Eurovision is held every year in May, with member countries submitting one original song. Over the years, the event’s format has changed from an exclusive jury vote to a viewer televote and today’s combination of both. Sometimes, voting can become political , with viewers voting according to their geopolitical preferences or diaspora communities casting ballots for their former home countries regardless of the quality of the performance. This may be good news for Canada, which is currently basking in European affection. The current geopolitical romance between Canada and the EU could help a Canadian song win. It wouldn’t be the first Canadian win, though. Céline Dion took home the prize in 1988 , representing Switzerland. Uranium fears in the 1950s The EU and Canada are clearly getting closer. But will historians look back at Eurovision and other developments as the beginning of comprehensive Canada-EU integration? Probably not — and history shows why. A look at the history of Canada-EU relations reveals a shared interest in deeper integration that has rarely materialized into anything concrete. More than half a century ago, a couple of years after the 1957 Treaty of Rome had established the European Economic Community and the European Atomic Energy Community , Canada was the first industrialized country to sign an agreement with the latter organization. In October 1959, Canada became a signatory to the Peaceful Uses of Atomic Energy deal. At the time, Canada was worried about losing the United States as a major export market for its uranium. That’s because the U.S. had only agreed to a supply contract until 1962, expecting much lower demand for Canadian uranium after that. Prime Minister John Diefenbaker, who wanted to diversify Canada’s trade relations and revive imperial links with the United Kingdom, looked to Europe for future uranium markets . He added Germany and Italy to the list of countries to buy Canadian uranium. Canada also tried to ensure these new customers would only use the uranium for peaceful purposes. To do so, Canada considered an agreement with the European Atomic Energy Community, of which both West Germany and Italy were member states, as the best option. For its part, the organization believed the agreement with Canada not only provided access to Canadian uranium and civilian nuclear technology but also gave it international visibility. But in retrospect, beyond scientific collaboration, not much else was achieved . Canada had already lost the race to the U.S., whose aggressive export policy led to Western Europe adopting American nuclear technology. Nixon-Trudeau tensions Diversification away from the U.S. was also behind the 1976 framework agreement for commercial and economic co-operation , which Canada signed as the first industrialized country with the European Community , which later became the European Union. Canada was surprised by U.S. President Richard Nixon’s 1971 announcement of a new economic program that abolished the conversion of gold to American dollars and terminated fixed exchange rates. Richard Nixon and Pierre Trudeau talk in Trudeau’s office in Ottawa in this April 1972 photo. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Chuck Mitchell Canada hadn’t been warned about the immediate imposition of a unilateral 10 per cent surcharge on imports, and it wasn’t exempted. In response to these Nixon shocks and fuelled by long-simmering anxieties about Canadian independence, the Liberal government under Pierre Trudeau proposed a third option to reduce dependence on the U.S. and actively seek new partnerships, mostly with Europe. As they did in the late 1950s, the Europeans were receptive to Canadian advances because they wanted access to Canada’s energy resources . This was especially true in the wake of the 1973 oil crisis, which had not only caused Western European countries to desperately search for oil supplies outside the Middle East and the Soviet Union, but also led to their heightened demands for uranium as nuclear power programs ramped up to provide alternative energy. But the framework agreement between Canada and European countries never realized its full potential. Instead, Canada deepened its relations with the U.S. and signed a free-trade agreement in the 1980s . Can momentum be sustained? Today, Canada faces another trade crisis with the U.S. Canadian oil and gas is in high demand, even in a decarbonizing Europe that’s cut off from Russian supplies. In addition, the current nuclear renaissance , the combined result of climate change action and fossil fuel geopolitics, has made Canada’s uranium a highly sought-after resource. No wonder the EU and Canada are seemingly moving closer. But will the rhetoric around middle power solidarity and common values be enough to sustain the momentum? Europeans and Canadians have always seen each other as friends, and Canada’s Eurovision participation will only cement that war relationship. But historically, closer ties have not led to deeper integration in the long run. Petra Dolata receives funding from the Social Sciences and Research Council of Canada, Environment and Climate Change Canada and the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung Kanada.

articles.content: As Halloween approaches and screen audiences are saturated with the sights and sounds of screaming women in horror films and TV shows, it’s a great time to look at the women whose vocal artistry created genuinely effective screams on screen. Behind every memorable cinematic scream lies a vocal performance that is often reduced to a natural, unreflective outburst. But that assessment obscures the women behind its most powerful manifestations. For example, think of the work of Shelley Duvall in The Shining , Janet Leigh in Psycho or Toni Collette in Hereditary . Certain screen actors have made the scream their calling card to fame and notoriety, under the designation “ scream queen .” These queens are the unsung heroes of the horror industry through their dedication to the vocal performance of the fear and terror in the many guises of horror. Long live the (scream) queen As onscreen horror proliferated in the 1970s, the term “scream queen” became popular, most notably through Calvin Beck’s 1978 book Scream Queens: Heroines of the Horrors . Later, in popular culture, “scream queen” applied to “ any female star who has made a career playing women who survive extreme trauma or peril .” Hollywood actress Jamie Lee Curtis qualifies to bear the mantle of “scream queen,” alongside others like Lin Shaye , Brinke Stevens , Michelle Bauer , and Linnea Quigley . While Curtis is well-known, the other actors may be less familiar even though they collectively have hundreds of film credits to their names , predominantly in low-budget horror productions. Those films occupy a robust and commercially significant segment of the film market. The market has shown remarkable resilience, even during the COVID-19 pandemic that saw a spike in people watching horror films . A trailer for the 2018 film, ‘Hereditary,’ starring Toni Collette. The onscreen scream Screen horror has relied on the scream as a sonic marker since the advent of sound film, and even earlier in the form of the silent scream . Screaming is a non-linguistic vocalization, like laughing and crying, rooted in ancient neural systems associated with survival. Its distinctive acoustic properties can engage subcortical mechanisms of threat detection, triggering heightened vigilance and lending the scream a particular communicative immediacy . Filmmakers exploit the scream’s capacity to evoke terror, but it can also express delight at a surprising revelation (the announcement of the band Donna and the Dynamos in Mamma Mia! ) or amusement over a comedic situation (when cross-dressing Robin Williams’ fake breasts catch fire in Mrs. Doubtfire ). It can likewise signify pain, most notoriously embodied in the male “ Wilhelm scream ” that has found use in more than 400 films, including Star Wars and the Lord of the Rings . Not all screams evoke terror. In this scene from Mamma Mia!, at 00:48:00, a delightful scream takes place. Fay Wray: The original scream queen Cinema of the early 1930s is rife with examples of horror, including Frankenstein (1931), Dracula (1931), The Mummy (1932) and King Kong (1933). It was in King Kong , however, that the prototype of the scream queen emerged through the vocal artistry of Fay Wray . As she later recalled in her autobiography , Wray entered an RKO sound studio before the film was edited to record a repertoire of screams and moans for insertion into the soundtrack — she called it an “aria of agonies.” Her screaming voice was heard in several other horror films of the time, establishing her reputation as the imperilled heroine, a historical precedent to later scream queens. Wray’s screams in King Kong subsequently entered the repertoire of sound effects (re-)deployed by sound engineers , reinforcing her status as a progenitor of the scream queen. Fay Wray in RKO’s 1933 King Kong. (RKO pictures) Empowering modern scream queens As horror cinema exploded into commercial prominence during the 1980s and ‘90s, the scream queen became one of horror’s defining female figures. Jamie Lee Curtis’ performance in Halloween (1978) was decisive not only for her career but for the evolution of the modern horror film and its female protagonist. Alongside Curtis, other scream queens like Linnea Quigley, Michelle Bauer and Brinke Stevens, whose names are less well known, emerged. They helped move the genre from the “final girl” model toward a fusion of horror, camp and sex appeal. The final girl refers to the trope of the last woman standing in a horror film; she’s the one who finally takes on the villain. Still, Curtis’s final girl proved enduring, evolving from a vulnerable survivor in 1978 into a formidable older heroine in the Halloween franchise’s later instalments. The shift toward female strength is exemplified by the career of Lin Shaye , whose work has appeared in more than 100 films over a span of 50 years. Shaye challenged the scream queen’s traditional association with youth and sexualized representations. She was most recently associated with the Insidious franchise, where she has served as the protagonist, psychic medium Elise Rainier. Recognizing that “ people attribute growing older to authority ,” Shaye has redefined the conventions of the scream queen through her portrayal of an older heroine whose experience, knowledge and agency become sources of power. Her body of work reflects an ongoing resistance to constraints that age, gender and genre might impose on her. She believes people want “ to see a person…have strength rather than be a victim .” Although Shaye continues to perform the screams associated with the genre, her portrayal of Rainier privileges authority over vulnerability, transforming the scream queen from a terrorized victim into an empowered agent. A trailer for ‘Insidious: The Last Key’ with Elise Rainer (Sony Pictures). A new era of scream queens As the scream queen transforms from vulnerability to empowerment, another change is in the works. Historically, the scream queen casts were almost entirely white women . This raises the question: What kinds of bodies are privileged to scream on screen? A diverse cast of scream queens may be making their way onto screens. Recent horror movies have introduced a new generation of scream queens to the cultural zeitgeist. Actress Jenna Ortega has been called “Gen-Z’s Scream Queen” , with her high-profile characters in _ Wednesday _, X , and Insidious . Her work has been applauded for her raw emotion, strength and animalistic vocalizations . Jenna Ortega in ‘Scream.’ (Paramount) Ortega’s work, alongside that of British actress Mia Goth , signals a shift in the genre. These women have made greater space for racially diverse and complex representations of women in horror. From victim to agent, the scream queen continues to draw and influence audiences. The scream was never just a simple reflex; it’s always been an artful cry. articles.content: Halloween, the fall holiday and $13.5 billion industry , lurks around the corner. But what’s behind the more than 11,000 acres of pumpkin patches across Canada and $3.9 billion in consumer spending on candy alone? Halloween has ancient origins in the pre-Christian religion and practices of the Celts . It was custom to honour the transitions between the seasons and harvest, acknowledge the thin veil between different planes of existence and also to commemorate the dead. Modern-day commercialization has shifted how people experience Halloween, but the spirits of the dead continue to play a significant role in the occasion and the time of year. The day’s appeal and its marketability extends beyond a one-day “holiday.” Many people are drawn to carefully curated encounters, seeking thrilling yet sanitized experiences that allow them to engage with the macabre and mortality from a safe distance. Consequently, Halloween’s commercial success in commodifying dread and the monstrous can be analyzed alongside broader “dark tourism” — an umbrella term that explores tourism involvement with sites of death, disaster and a difficult heritage. Anthropologist Philip Stone notes that a range of motivations exist for promoting engagement with death, disaster and the macabre : for example, political reasons or remembrance, education, entertainment or economic gain. So how should we think about worldwide Halloween-related attractions that not only seek to entertain but also promote interpretation and engagement with sites marketed as scary, which often have genuinely dark pasts? Prisons, forts For example, a tourism attraction at Eastern State Penitentiary — a former prison in Philadelphia — markets itself as a Halloween festival of epic proportions . The onetime prison was an 11-acre institution that was the first jail in the United States to introduce the practice of solitary confinement in the late 1800s. In the late ‘90s, the property switched gears, launched “terror behind the walls” as an annual haunted house and then rebranded as “ Halloween Nights .” The facility notes that proceeds from Halloween Nights benefit a mission to preserve the site and advance “public understanding of the criminal justice system and its impact on the lives of those affected by it [and] to inspire a more just future,” including through public education and exhibits . Another example is Fort Henry in Kingston, Ont. Although Fort Henry was never a battlefield site, it was the site of an 1838 execution . It was also used as a prison for combatants captured during the 1837-38 Rebellions in Upper and Lower Canada and again during the First and Second World Wars for “civilian enemy aliens.” Today, coffin rides and a monster shooting range are part of the Heritage Sites tourist attraction called Fort Fright , which simulates a haunted attraction and experience throughout the month of October leading up to Halloween. Historical educational programming exists through the year. These types of attractions are examples of fright tourism , when people seek scares and thrills for pleasure at a destination that may have a sinister history or is promoted as having one. Other forts have also offered similar experiences timed to Halloween . Urban ghost stories Urban ghost stories also continue to spark interest, both at Halloween and at other times. The Lost Souls of Gastown Tour , a performance-theatre experience in Vancouver, is one example. Visitors participating in the tour immerse themselves in the city’s stories of crime, disaster, historical figures and hidden urban spaces. Victoria Ghost Walking Tours offers a tour touching on “horrible deeds” and other eerie experiences for folks on Vancouver Island, as do other cities. Important questions raised Why do people seek fear if it’s associated with danger? Why do tourists travel for entertainment or fun to places with tragic or apparently haunted pasts, sometimes associated with horrible, disturbing or traumatic events? Although fear is fundamentally a warning mechanism that alerts us to potential danger, it also generates the release of adrenaline. In settings where people perceive themselves to be safe, this tension between threat and security can become an appealing experience . Stone analyzes dark tourism along a spectrum. The “darkest” end of the spectrum is characterized by experiences pertaining to education and authentic sites where death and suffering happened. The “lighter” end is “heritage-centric,” with an entertainment orientation perceived as inauthentic and more associated with tourism. Many Halloween-themed sites and experiences are arguably situated on the lighter end of the dark tourism spectrum and marketed as entertainment. As mentioned, some are linked to real experiences or engage with stories or sites associated with death, social control, crime and disaster. Ethical boundaries? Researchers studying dark tourism in prison museums have noted that people’s interactions in these spaces demonstrate that “not all dark experiences are equally 'dark’ to all visitors.” This means that sites cannot dictate how their curated experiences will be received. This suggests it’s important to pay close attention to the ethical boundaries between interpretation and entertainment. When these boundaries are blurred, the dignity of victims can be compromised while the educational and commemorative value of historic sites may be diminished. This raises important questions about the responsibilities of tourism providers when presenting difficult and often painful histories, and, as Stone also examines, their relationship to political ideology. Read more: A prison is no place for a party Some argue the boundary between a tourism attraction and the site of a traumatic past can become nuanced — for example, when former prisons, as attraction sites, provide educational resources for visitors . All attractions situated along the dark tourism spectrum, whether they lean toward the “lighter” or “darker” end, must carefully navigate the line between respectful engagement and exploitation. This is particularly relevant for Halloween tourism experiences that draw upon stories or sites that intersect with crime, death or tragedy. When attractions encourage visitors to engage with local history, they should not glorify perpetrators , sensationalize violence or trivialize suffering. In these cases, exhibit operators should prioritize historically grounded narratives that provide context, acknowledge victims and encourage reflection. This may be a daunting challenge. articles.content: As the days darken, making more room for arts-based practices and experiences is one way to bring useful, interesting or sustaining activities into the seasons ahead. For families and people working in schools, this may be particularly relevant as the school year settles into its routines and demands. Making more room for the arts can expand the resources available to students , families and educators, including opportunities for curiosity, connection and enjoyment in daily life. Even positive or eagerly anticipated changes require us to adapt , which can take attention, time and emotional energy. What requires little thought once it becomes habitual can require considerable attention when new. Our capacity to navigate these changes is shaped by the resources available to us and the relationships and systems we are part of. A student who was excited to be back at school may stumble with figuring out new friendships, expectations or responsibilities, while another may feel the dread that can emerge after difficult experiences or alongside boredom and uncertainty. Parents and caregivers support these day-to-day challenges alongside everything else they carry and manage, while teachers lead classrooms within school systems where time, staffing and other resources are often stretched thin . Art to expand our resources As an art therapist, my work generally begins when someone is already struggling. This has led me to consider what happens further upstream: what experiences, relationships and resources might become part of everyday life before difficulties become overwhelming? Everyday art-making is not art therapy, nor is it a substitute for professional support when needed. But a growing body of research suggests that arts engagement can contribute to health and well-being , including social and personal dimensions of well-being in educational settings . Making room for creative activities in schools can give students additional opportunities to explore their interests and express themselves. (Unsplash) Making and experiencing art can expand the resources people have available and help them discover capacities they may draw on in other parts of their lives. While creative practices can help expand the ways we express or comfort ourselves in difficult moments, they can also bring curiosity, imagination, connection and enjoyment into ordinary days. Read more: For both artists and scientists, slow looking allows surprising connections to surface Something interesting and pleasurable Sometimes, the value of making art simply lies in being absorbed in something interesting or pleasurable. Like exercise, reading or other activities that sustain us, engaging with the arts does not have to begin with a problem that needs solving. I am focusing here on visual art, though music, theatre, dance, writing and other creative practices may be more inviting depending on people’s interests and affinities. One common obstacle is the expectation of being “good” at art right away. Artistic skills and visual languages can be learned and explored , with people bringing different strengths, ways of learning and interests to them . Making art will not appeal to everyone, but deciding it is “not for you” because it does not come easily at first can mean giving up something you might enjoy. Most people who enjoy cycling will never compete in the Tour de France, nor would they want to; the pleasure and value of cycling do not depend on reaching that level of ability. Getting lost in doodling can take the imagination somewhere else. Knitting or beading can offer repetition and rhythm that feel welcome after a day filled with too many unknowns. Clay, collaging and painting engage the senses differently and offer room to experiment, play or express what is difficult to put into words. Photography can invite closer attention to our surroundings. None of these need to become a project, accomplishment or regular practice to have value. Creative resources can be kept within easy reach: a student might keep a container of putty among their school supplies, something tactile to turn to in a stressful moment. These resources need not disappear with childhood. A tired parent might appreciate their own ball of modelling clay during yet another Zoom meeting. Keeping creative corners accessible Experiencing the arts can spark curiosity, introduce experiences beyond our own, or let us encounter something of our own experience in another person’s work. Access to the arts can be built into places people already spend time. A creative corner in a school staff room could offer materials to explore and opportunities for colleagues to connect differently during a break. Libraries, museums, galleries and community centres offer inexpensive or free ways to engage with the arts . Making these experiences accessible is important, particularly when time, money, space or access to materials can limit people’s options. Building capacity also means looking beyond what individuals can do for themselves to what resources families, schools and communities can make available. What we make available to one another is also part of how we build care and support into our environments. Making more room for the arts is one way to do this. Through all seasons, we can think beyond what needs to be accomplished and build in more of what can help people stay connected, engaged and resourced.
