articles.content: When the Swedish Academy announced Anne Carson as the recipient of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature , in Stockholm, I was participating in a panel discussion in the same city at Stockholm University about possible laureates — and the literary traditions they represent. Before the announcement, I had spoken about two Canadian writers, Margaret Atwood and Carson , whose international recognition reflects different trajectories within contemporary literature. Carson’s work challenges the very categories through which we usually classify literary achievement. It moves between poetry, translation, philosophical reflection and the reconfiguration of ancient myths. The Swedish Academy justified its decision by praising Carson’s “bold and inventive oeuvre” and its “playful dialogue with the classical tradition” that have allowed her to create new forms for contemporary literature. This formulation captures a fundamental paradox of her writing: Carson’s literary modernity emerges from a persistent return to antiquity , not as a stable cultural inheritance to be preserved, but as an unfinished reservoir of images, voices and fragments capable of unsettling contemporary experience. Meaning of fragments Fragments of ancient text occupy a privileged position in Carson’s literary universe. These establish a connection between the material survival of ancient texts and the discontinuous forms associated with modern and postmodern writing. ‘If not, Winter: Fragments of Sappho’ translation by Anne Carson. (Penguin Random House) Carson’s translation of Sappho’s surviving poetry in If Not, Winter (2002) exemplifies this approach. Carson preserves the gaps and interruptions of the original fragments, rather than attempting to disguise them through speculative reconstruction. The resulting poems make absence visible, allowing silence and discontinuity to participate in the production of meaning. This attention to what remains incomplete establishes an unexpected affinity between archaic poetry and modern literary experimentation. Fragmentation is frequently associated with the crisis of representation in 20th-century literature. Carson reveals that the ancient textual tradition already contains discontinuities that resist the modern desire for completeness. ‘Eros the Bittersweet’ This relationship between ancient thought and contemporary experimentation is central to Carson’s long essay Eros the Bittersweet (1986) . This work combines classical scholarship, philosophical inquiry and poetic reflection. Carson begins with the Greek understanding of eros as an experience that combines pleasure and suffering. She draws particular attention to Sappho’s description of desire as glukupikron , or bittersweet. Vase image depicting Sappho, from c. 470 BCE. (Wikimedia) , CC BY-SA The apparent contradiction contained within this expression becomes the starting point for an investigation into the structure of desire, which depends upon distance, incompleteness and the impossibility of fully possessing its object. Carson explores the fundamentally relational character of desire: Desire emerges in the interval separating the lover from the beloved. It is precisely this distance that generates both the intensity of attraction and the suffering associated with absence. Her reading of ancient Greek literature connects this paradox to the emergence of self-consciousness , since the experience of desiring another person also reveals the limits of the self. The beloved remains irreducibly other. The attempt to overcome this separation exposes the impossibility of complete identification. Carson’s treatment of eros also reveals what might be called an archaic drive within her postmodern writing, provided that the term is understood as the persistence of fundamental human experiences that resist closure, not as nostalgia for an idealized past. Desire, vulnerability and the confrontation with absence return through ancient metaphors, while their literary expression is continually renewed by contemporary forms. In this sense, Carson is a philosopher who works through metaphors, allowing poetic language to produce concepts rather than merely illustrate ideas established elsewhere. ‘Autobiography of Red’ The philosophical reflections developed in Eros the Bittersweet acquire a remarkable narrative form in Autobiography of Red (1998) . This novel in verse reconfigures the ancient myth of Geryon, the red-winged monster defeated by Herakles. Carson draws upon the surviving fragments of the Greek poet Stesichorus , whose account of Geryon belongs to a mythological tradition organized around the heroic exploits of Herakles. Yet Carson shifts the narrative perspective towards Geryon himself, rather than reproducing the familiar opposition between the victorious hero and the monstrous adversary. This shift transforms a figure traditionally defined through his defeat into the protagonist of an intimate exploration of identity, desire and emotional vulnerability. This reversal is significant because it changes the moral and narrative structure of the ancient myth. The monster becomes a subject capable of remembering , suffering, loving and reflecting upon his own difference. He is no longer simply the embodiment of an external threat against which heroic identity can be established. The relationship between Geryon and Herakles also reconfigures the ancient narrative through the language of contemporary sexuality and emotional experience. Their intimacy is marked by attraction, separation and the unequal experience of desire. This recalls the philosophical paradox examined in Eros the Bittersweet : love is sustained by an irreducible distance between individuals, even when they seek closeness. What emerges is not simply a modernized version of Greek mythology, but a transformation of the relationship between heroism and monstrosity. By granting Geryon an autobiographical voice, Carson questions the authority of inherited narratives and the distribution of visibility within the classical tradition. The novel’s poetic form reinforces this instability through the co-existence of lyric intensity, narrative development, visual imagery and reflections on the act of representation. Ancient sources, postmodern insight? To describe Carson’s work as postmodern may initially seem paradoxical, given the centrality of ancient Greek literature to her intellectual formation. Yet this apparent contradiction is precisely what makes her writing distinctive. She uses some of the most recognizable techniques of postmodern literature — intertextuality, hybrid genres, disrupted chronology and unstable narrative authority — to reactivate experiences and symbolic structures inherited from antiquity. In this way, Carson examines anew forms of experience that continue to inhabit contemporary culture: desire, loss, violence, otherness and the limits of language. Reinvention of literary forms The Swedish Academy’s recognition of Carson invites us to reconsider the relationship between literary tradition and innovation. As a Canadian writer deeply connected to ancient Greek literature, Carson resists what could be understood as conventional classifications of national literary identity — though Carson, also a member of the Order of Canada and an awarded poet in the country , has also inspired questions about Canadian literature and culture . Carson’s Nobel Prize recognizes not simply the survival of classical literature within contemporary writing, but the capacity of ancient fragments to generate new literary possibilities. articles.content: Canadian poet and author Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize for literature . The honour comes in the midst of Canada’s literary prize season and provides some clues into how Canadian talent finds an international audience. Carson , born in Toronto, moves between poetry, essay, translation, classics and drama, often challenging the boundaries separating these forms. Read more: Anne Carson wins Nobel prize in literature – how she discovered new possibilities within language Anne Carson at the 2024 National Book Awards finalist reading in the NYU Skirball Center in New York. (Jay Dixit/Wikimedia) , CC BY-SA Her reputation has developed through institutions associated particularly with poetry and experimental literature, including the Griffin Poetry Prize , the T.S. Eliot Prize, a MacArthur Fellowship and Spain’s Princess of Asturias Award for Literature . articles.content: The September 2026 removal of a sculpture from the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., has prompted criticism. The move is understood by arts activists as reflecting United States President Donald Trump’s wider efforts to appropriate and rebrand the Center and curtail modern styles at federal facilities. The Associated Press reports that a “Trump-aligned board” at the Center is fighting in court for the right to put Trump’s name on the historic institution . Read more: Trump has gotten rid of many of the checks and balances that could stop him from demolishing the Kennedy Center Trump took aim at “modernist” architecture and promoted “traditional” and “classical” structures in two executive orders issued in 2020 and 2025 . The group Hands Off the Arts , described the decision to remove artist Joel Shapiro’s sculpture Blue as “ authoritarian ” and as an act of “ vandalism .” The large blue geometric sculpture playfully evoked the human form in motion. Born in 1941, the late Shapiro was known for bridging modernism and postmodernism with sculptures that combined minimalist abstraction with figuration and movement. The abstract sculpture was removed from the Kennedy Center and follows executive orders from U.S. President Donald Trump to promote ‘traditional’ and ‘classical’ structures. (Jeff Vincent/Flickr) , CC BY In addition to the Kennedy Center, Trump has sought to transform Washington D.C. in other ways. His demolition of the East Wing of the White House, repainting of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and plans to build a new triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery have all raised questions about legal and regulatory limits on presidential actions impacting cultural heritage. Read more: Trump wants an ‘Independence Arch’ — How famous arches warn about dangers to republics Outside of Washington D.C., work on the border wall between the U.S. and Mexico has damaged and continues to threaten Indigenous archaeological and sacred sites . Trump’s attempts to dismantle , politicize and take over public institutions for arts and learning have been well documented. Such attacks on cultural heritage in the U.S. are not unique. In recent years, several governments have placed at risk the very heritage they are charged to protect. Cultural policy and state control International law places primary responsibility for protecting cultural heritage on states. The U.S. proposed the World Heritage Convention to the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) in 1972 and was the first state to ratify it . According to the convention , each state party to it “recognizes that the duty of ensuring the identification, protection, conservation, presentation and transmission to future generations of the cultural and natural heritage … belongs primarily to that State.” But recent research suggests attacks on cultural heritage and institutions are sometimes part of democratic backsliding and broader strategies to normalize political corruption and institute authoritarian policies. Trump and his administration have repeatedly criticized UNESCO, accusing the UN agency that seeks to safeguard heritage of supporting “woke, divisive cultural and social causes.” Trump withdrew the U.S. from UNESCO in 2019. The U.S. rejoined UNESCO in 2023 under the administration of former president Joe Biden . But the U.S. is slated to withdraw from the UN agency once again at the end of 2026 . Russia: Trinity icon Contested state decisions impacting culture and heritage can be seen elsewhere. In 2023, curators warned that Russian president Vladimir Putin’s plans to transfer a masterpiece of 15th-century Russian religious art from the State Tretyakov Gallery to the Russian Orthodox Church would put it at risk. Experts cautioned that removing Andrei Rublev’s Trinity icon from its climate-controlled museum case would likely damage it, a scenario that has now unfolded, according to a report from RBC media outlet publicized in the Moscow Times and the Art Newspaper in September 2026. Painted in the 1420s, Rublev’s icon is widely regarded as a treasure of Russian cultural heritage and one of the greatest examples of Orthodox icon painting. Putin’s transfer of the icon to the church in 2023 has been interpreted as politically motivated : a recognition of the loyalty of Patriarch Kirill, leader of the Russian Orthodox Church, who has steadfastly supported Russia’s war against Ukraine. Turkish case: Hagia Sophia In Turkey, five years ago, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan removed the museum status of Istanbul’s Hagia Sophia and converted it back into a mosque. Built in the sixth century on a site occupied by earlier churches since the fourth century CE, Hagia Sophia was the largest and most important church of the Greek-speaking Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire for nearly a millennium. It was converted into a mosque following the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453. In 1934 it was a made a museum by the founder of the Turkish Republic Mustafa Kemal Atatürk who sought to establish Turkey as a modern secular state. Hagia Sophia remains a singular masterpiece of Byzantine architecture and preserves unique mosaics of Roman rulers and Christian saints. It became part of the UNESCO World Heritage Historic Areas of Istanbul in 1985. In 2022, reports emerged that heavy machinery used for cleaning had cracked marble floor slabs inside Hagia Sophia. Hagia Sophia is one of several former Byzantine-era churches in Turkey that Erdoğan has converted into mosques in recent years. These acts have been seen as attempts by Erdoğan, amid wider strategies, to shore up support from his conservative Muslim base and represss political opposition . The conversion of Hagia Sophia has been opposed by scholars , museum workers and world leaders . UNESCO stressed the universal value of Hagia Sophia’s heritage and said it “deeply regrets” Turkey’s decision to strip Hagia Sophia of its museum status without prior consultation. Interior of Hagia Sophia following its conversion back to a mosque. (Sourabh.biswas003/Wikimedia) , CC BY-SA State-centred frameworks Over the course of the 20th century, NGOs, Indigenous Peoples, religious groups and local communities have played a growing role in the conservation and protection of cultural heritage. Their participation has gained increasing recognition in international cultural heritage law. UNESCO acknowledges that the protection of cultural heritage “cannot rest on State Parties alone” and that representatives of civil society can “strengthen conservation, foster awareness and education, empower local communities and offer independent monitoring when challenges arise.” In addition to established understandings of intrinsic esthetic and historic values of heritage, new emphasis on development reconceptualizes heritage as a resource that can generate economic development, tourism, employment and social cohesion. But legal frameworks remain largely state-centred, often limiting what civilian groups can accomplish without state co-operation. These developments raise the question: How can cultural heritage be protected when the state threatens rather than safeguards it? articles.content: The recently published thriller The Most Dangerous Games is a collaboration between James Stephen “Jimmy” Donaldson, better known as MrBeast, and popular author James Patterson. It tells the story of 100 contestants competing for US$1 billion while enduring an escalation of increasingly brutal challenges. The publisher explicitly markets the book as an extension of his Prime Original program Beast Games : “the games are more dangerous than ever.” Each book purchase gets the buyer a chance to enter an online game and potentially compete for US$1 million. The book is the latest extension of a format MrBeast developed on YouTube years before Beast Games reached television. Beginning with challenges such as “ Last To Leave Circle Wins $10,000 ” in 2018, his videos increasingly centred on contestants competing for large cash prizes. The promotional language for Beast Games puts it bluntly: What wouldn’t you do for $5 million? When money becomes the spectacle The idea of making people confront their fears for money is not new to reality television. Joe Rogan hosted Fear Factor from 2001 to 2006, putting groups of contestants through three stunts for a chance to win US$50,000. The program opens with the words: “ imagine a world where your greatest fears become reality .” But contestants were not forced to confront common fears such as public speaking or cold-calling strangers. Instead, the program traded in shock, disgust and spectacle. Despite being revived twice after its initial cancellation, Fear Factor did not acquire the longevity of other reality formats in which contestants compete for cash. Survivor , for example, has just celebrated its 50th season, while The Amazing Race has produced nearly 40. Unlike these programs, Fear Factor was gimmicky and vulnerable to a shrinking audience once the novelty wore off. There was no real way for the show to evolve beyond its basic format. Even Joe Rogan admitted he expected it to be cancelled quickly and mainly took the job to gather material for his stand-up comedy career. The reality competition series ‘Fear Factor’ made fear, disgust and spectacle central to its format. In one challenge, contestants were strapped down and covered with dozens of snakes for three minutes. Long-running reality competition programs like Survivor and Big Brother clearly demonstrate that viewers are fascinated by watching people compete for financial gain. The reason for this is obvious. We like money; it facilitates survival and we all wish we had more of it. But not all competitions are equal, and neither are the reasons people watch them . While Fear Factor is now mainly a footnote in reality TV history (it did get rebooted again in January 2026 ), it was notable in part for making money itself the spectacle. For contemporary viewers, no one does this more obviously than MrBeast. Competition or ordeal? The level of spectacle in Beast Games is very different from competition shows where the money is structurally important but narratively sidelined. While the ostensible objective in Survivor is to win US$1 million, the format converts that goal into something more complicated for the audience. Viewers become invested in strategy, social relationships, general competence, travel, personality and questions of deservingness. The pleasure of watching goes far beyond “look what this person will do for this money.” James Patterson and MrBeast’s ‘The Most Dangerous Games’ extends the MrBeast competition format into fiction. (William Morrow and Company) Beast Games does not provoke debates about who can or should win and how. Rather, it stages a demonstration of what money can make people agree to. This helps explain to what extent Beast Games is inspired by the Korean drama Squid Game , which depicts desperate people submitting themselves to degrading and dangerous conditions to win money. The willingness of the Squid Game contestants to return to the games, even once they realize that the outcome could be deadly, is an indictment of the pervasive economic precarity that is sadly familiar to many viewers. This functions as a profound, and at times even moving, critique. Beast Games , however, exploits this precarity and turns it back into mere entertainment. While traditional reality competition shows ask, “Can you out-game the other players and win the money?”, Beast Games explores how much you will endure – or subject someone else to – for a transformative financial sum. This distinction between competition and ordeal can be deepened when we consider the roles played by precarity, humiliation and spectatorship . Humiliation as entertainment The spectacle of humiliation is hardly new. In entertainment it is an ancient practice, tracing as far back as slaves in the Roman Colosseum engaging in deadly competition while spectators placed bets on the outcome . Early reality programs were frequently accused of being exploitative. American Idol showcased terrible auditions and mocking judges, while Big Brother confined and surveilled contestants. Survivor continues to foreground deprivation as part of the journey to becoming sole survivor. In its early years, it featured its own share of Fear Factor -style food challenges . Yet over time, the pleasure of watching many of these legacy programs has shifted from schadenfreude to inspiration. MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, has built his online career around elaborate challenges and cash prizes. (Amazon MGM Studios) The key to this transformation is in the different ways these experiences are organized and made productively legible to viewers. Big Brother turns confinement into social observation. Survivor builds a mythology of adventure and strategic gameplay on top of deprivation and personality conflicts. The popular social deduction game, The Traitors , is a relative newcomer to the world of reality competition shows, but it has quickly established itself as an international favourite. Traitors stages a theatrical parlour game in which everyone is actively “pretending.” Building the prize pot is secondary to the often conflicting goals of finding traitors and getting to the end. The MrBeast approach strips away much of this genre’s camouflage and positions the enormous pile of money as central to the mise-en-scène . The business of desperation This is where Squid Game offers an uncomfortable comparison. The drama was supposed to make us uneasy with watching desperate people endure unsavoury ordeals for transformative wealth. Yet it has helped establish the aesthetic vocabulary for unironic real competitions like Beast Games . Read more: ‘Squid Game’ highlights plight of South Korean workers sacrificed for nation’s economic gain The class distinction is particularly apparent when the money on offer is framed as coming directly from MrBeast himself, as an altruistic gesture for which he is celebrated. In reality, this money comes primarily from sponsors . Even if we take the premise at face value, it remains uncomfortably reminiscent of a familiar scenario in which people in financial need become fodder for the entertainment of the wealthy. Not unlike the infamous Bumfights series, it asks: What can someone with relative wealth induce needy people to do by dangling enough money in front of them? The more difficult question, however, might be: Why are humiliation, fear and economic need seen as entertainment? Unlike these programs, Fear Factor was gimmicky and vulnerable to a shrinking audience once the novelty wore off. There was no real way for the show to evolve beyond its basic format. Even Joe Rogan admitted he expected it to be cancelled quickly and mainly took the job to gather material for his stand-up comedy career. The reality competition series ‘Fear Factor’ made fear, disgust and spectacle central to its format. In one challenge, contestants were strapped down and covered with dozens of snakes for three minutes. Long-running reality competition programs like Survivor and Big Brother clearly demonstrate that viewers are fascinated by watching people compete for financial gain. The reason for this is obvious. We like money; it facilitates survival and we all wish we had more of it. But not all competitions are equal, and neither are the reasons people watch them . While Fear Factor is now mainly a footnote in reality TV history (it did get rebooted again in January 2026 ), it was notable in part for making money itself the spectacle. For contemporary viewers, no one does this more obviously than MrBeast. Competition or ordeal? The level of spectacle in Beast Games is very different from competition shows where the money is structurally important but narratively sidelined. While the ostensible objective in Survivor is to win US$1 million, the format converts that goal into something more complicated for the audience. Viewers become invested in strategy, social relationships, general competence, travel, personality and questions of deservingness. The pleasure of watching goes far beyond “look what this person will do for this money.” James Patterson and MrBeast’s ‘The Most Dangerous Games’ extends the MrBeast competition format into fiction. (William Morrow and Company) Beast Games does not provoke debates about who can or should win and how. Rather, it stages a demonstration of what money can make people agree to. This helps explain to what extent Beast Games is inspired by the Korean drama Squid Game , which depicts desperate people submitting themselves to degrading and dangerous conditions to win money. The willingness of the Squid Game contestants to return to the games, even once they realize that the outcome could be deadly, is an indictment of the pervasive economic precarity that is sadly familiar to many viewers. This functions as a profound, and at times even moving, critique. Beast Games , however, exploits this precarity and turns it back into mere entertainment. While traditional reality competition shows ask, “Can you out-game the other players and win the money?”, Beast Games explores how much you will endure – or subject someone else to – for a transformative financial sum. This distinction between competition and ordeal can be deepened when we consider the roles played by precarity, humiliation and spectatorship . Humiliation as entertainment The spectacle of humiliation is hardly new. In entertainment it is an ancient practice, tracing as far back as slaves in the Roman Colosseum engaging in deadly competition while spectators placed bets on the outcome . Early reality programs were frequently accused of being exploitative. American Idol showcased terrible auditions and mocking judges, while Big Brother confined and surveilled contestants. Survivor continues to foreground deprivation as part of the journey to becoming sole survivor. In its early years, it featured its own share of Fear Factor -style food challenges . Yet over time, the pleasure of watching many of these legacy programs has shifted from schadenfreude to inspiration. MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, has built his online career around elaborate challenges and cash prizes. (Amazon MGM Studios) The key to this transformation is in the different ways these experiences are organized and made productively legible to viewers. Big Brother turns confinement into social observation. Survivor builds a mythology of adventure and strategic gameplay on top of deprivation and personality conflicts. The popular social deduction game, The Traitors , is a relative newcomer to the world of reality competition shows, but it has quickly established itself as an international favourite. Traitors stages a theatrical parlour game in which everyone is actively “pretending.” Building the prize pot is secondary to the often conflicting goals of finding traitors and getting to the end. The MrBeast approach strips away much of this genre’s camouflage and positions the enormous pile of money as central to the mise-en-scène . The business of desperation This is where Squid Game offers an uncomfortable comparison. The drama was supposed to make us uneasy with watching desperate people endure unsavoury ordeals for transformative wealth. Yet it has helped establish the aesthetic vocabulary for unironic real competitions like Beast Games . Read more: ‘Squid Game’ highlights plight of South Korean workers sacrificed for nation’s economic gain The class distinction is particularly apparent when the money on offer is framed as coming directly from MrBeast himself, as an altruistic gesture for which he is celebrated. In reality, this money comes primarily from sponsors . Even if we take the premise at face value, it remains uncomfortably reminiscent of a familiar scenario in which people in financial need become fodder for the entertainment of the wealthy. Not unlike the infamous Bumfights series, it asks: What can someone with relative wealth induce needy people to do by dangling enough money in front of them? The more difficult question, however, might be: Why are humiliation, fear and economic need seen as entertainment? articles.content: “Math rock” band Angine de Poitrine seems to be everywhere now: the Saguenay, Québec duo won two prestigious Polaris prizes on Sept. 22, and recently appeared on the United States-based Tonight Show and other international venues . The Polaris Prize honours important Canadian music and is adjudicated by over 200 critics and curators. Angine de Poitrine won both the album and song prizes. The latter is jointly awarded by Polaris and the Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada . The band became a viral sensation in early 2026 and has been performing sold-out shows around the globe . A significant part of the attention they have garnered is due to their outlandish stage presence and self-described status as an “anonymous art project” — guitarist “Khn” and drummer “Klek” wear polka-dotted outfits and giant papier mâché heads in the guise of being alien rock stars . Read more: Dada: how 1916 art movement reacting to world war is inspiring improvisation artists today But the band’s music, which features microtonal melodies, dense, elaborately constructed textures and wonky, complex rhythms, has also captured the attention of a legion of music fans. Just as the duo has dominated social media and the summer concert circuit, iconic Canadian progressive rock power trio Rush has been on a much-hyped, epic global reunion tour , marking almost 50 years in the music industry. Does their popularity suggest, improbably, that we are witnessing a progressive rock renaissance? Emergence of ‘prog rock’ In the late 1960s, shaped by developments in psychedelic rock especially, progressive rock (or “prog”) emerged as a rejection of commercial pop and blues-based rock music, borrowing from other musical traditions — art music, jazz, non-western music — and focusing on technical virtuosity, long-format songs, experimentation, quasi-symphonic textures and classical forms. Prog’s popularity declined precipitously in the mid ‘70s, and the genre — with its legendary excesses, including self-indulgent soloing, abstruse lyrics and pompous conceits — was eclipsed by the advent of punk. Rush played a key role in the development of prog. Forming in Toronto in 1968 and releasing its first album in 1974 , Rush blended heavy blues-based rock in the vein of Led Zeppelin, The Who and Cream with the richer palette offered by seminal British prog groups. The progressive aspects of Rush’s music have included atmospheric guitar textures, virtuosic melodic bass lines, technically demanding drum parts and the use of irregular meter (which instead of the usual multiples of four, sees the music grouped into “irregular” units of five or seven, for example). In the 1980s, this gave way to a more radio-friendly approach, leading to a succession of very successful, chart-topping Rush songs throughout the decade. Angine on the prog rock spectrum While Rush emerged from this “classic” prog era, Angine de Poitrine occupies a different part of the prog rock spectrum. The band’s music is typically described as math rock , a sub-genre of prog that originated in the early 1990s. Writer Jeff Gomez has traced its history in his recent monograph Math Rock , going back through free jazz, progressive rock and thrash metal. While there is no universal agreement on the meaning or value of the label “math rock,” it’s safe to say that it consists primarily of instrumental rock music that features virtuosic, highly precise playing and significant rhythmic and metrical complexity . The music not only makes use of irregular meter and phrases of irregular length — common in classic prog — but can also be polymetric, with simultaneous musical lines being counted in different time groupings. Angine de Poitrine perform at the Polaris Prize on Sept. 22, 2026. Layered, looped music parts In the case of Angine de Poitrine, the band’s guitarist plays a double-necked instrument that includes a bass guitar. Guitar and bass parts are performed in real time and looped . That is, the parts are recorded digitally as Khn plays them, and then they repeat in continuous circuits. Loop is layered on top of loop; the loops are different lengths, and are counted in different time groupings. The math of this music has to do with how the loops progress cyclically and eventually line up. The effect is kaleidoscopic, in that multiple melodic lines complete for the ear’s attention, and shift in and out of phase with each other, creating a succession of new relationships. It requires some elaborate choreography. The loop station and a cluster of volume pedals, which bring loops in and out of the mix, sit on the floor and are controlled by the guitarist’s feet. The drummer plays steadily against the polymetric guitar and bass parts, at times in tension with the guitar parts and then locked in when the parts align, creating some decidedly funky grooves. The new Rush? Is Angine de Poitrine really “the new Rush,” as some fans have claimed on social media? Can we compare these two bands and, if so, what can we say about the state of “progressive” music? While on tour, the members of Rush sang the praises of Angine de Poitrine , sensing some affinities between the duo and their own esthetic tradition. And the complexity of both Rush and Angine appeals directly to other musicians, who respect the challenges of composing this kind of music, and co-ordinating parts in live performance. But Rush’s prog rock pedigree is now also overwritten by a strong nostalgia element and by a legacy of radio-friendly songs that have become unchallenged fixtures in the classic rock firmament. Angine de Poitrine is undeniably impressive, and they are certainly exciting to hear and see live , but the costumes, “alien rock star” conceit and absence of singing could suggest a short shelf life. Building complex musical textures is no longer novel, with looping technology entering its third decade, and with math rock bands — like the San Francisco post-rock duo Giraffes? Giraffes! — making similar quirky, loop-driven music since the early 2000s. Ongoing boom of less commercial music Perhaps, then, we didn’t exactly see a prog rock renaissance in 2026. But in some ways, prog never really went away. Not only have bands like Rush carried on (for almost 50 years, alongside other still-active prog dinosaurs like Styx and Yes), but the prog rock impulse towards music that is less commercial, with more elaborate, long-format songwriting, has evolved. It can still be heard in the music of recent prog groups like Dream Theatre , Porcupine Tree , Big Big Train and Wobbler , but also in the music of more mainstream acts like Radiohead , Tool and Primus. Thanks to social media and streaming, commercial radio no longer dictates the forms of music production. The success of bands like Angine de Poitrine at least show that rock music can challenge our ears and doesn’t need to be dumbed down or Tik Tok-ified to find a huge and appreciative audience. articles.content: Shane Hollander (played by Hudson Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (played by Connor Storrie) face-off in a scene from 'Heated Rivlary.' (Sabrina Lantos/HBO Max) Hockey has made it big on the small screen. TV’s buzziest show, Heated Rivalry , debuted in late 2025, with Off Campus following in 2026. They join beloved Canadian show Shoresy , which has a sixth season going into production this fall . These shows all challenge traditional hockey culture in their own ways. Shoresy promotes an inclusive vision of hockey that includes women and Indigenous people in leadership positions. Heated Rivalry ‘s queer romance challenges the sport’s longstanding assumptions of heteronormativity . Off Campus highlights the issue of sexual assault within hockey . But as the NHL season begins, a series of controversies suggests that many of the sport’s longstanding cultural issues appear to remain unresolved. Hockey’s culture problem Hockey has long been associated with traditional ideas about masculinity, toughness and heterosexuality. The culture surrounding hockey has historically marginalized women and LGBTQ+ people. Sexist phrases like “puck bunny” are used to diminish female fans , while Hockey Canada’s 2022 discrimination report found that negative comments about sexual orientation and gender identity accounted for 61 per cent of incidents witnessed by officials. Players’ self-reported allegations were most commonly related to race, sexual orientation and gender identity. It is also one of the most expensive sports , with participation typically limited to families who can afford to spend thousands of dollars on equipment, league fees and travel costs. Players and managers in the NHL are predominantly white , with the league having the lowest level of player diversity among the four major North American professional sports leagues. We Breed Lions: Confronting Canada’s Troubled Hockey Culture by Rick Westhead. (Penguin Random House) These issues have become increasingly visible in recent years as hockey organizations have faced pressure to address questions about safety, inclusion and accountability . The publication of TSN reporter Rick Westhead’s book We Breed Lions further intensified national conversations about hockey culture. In it, Westhead documents sexual abuse and hazing in junior hockey and examines the sport’s impact on its players’ physical and mental health and its growing exclusivity. The book demonstrates that these issues are systemic, not isolated incidents. We need to address the culture that encourages such behaviour and the way teammates, coaches and other personnel are complicit. Recent controversies The 2025 NHL season and 2026 summer off-season saw a number of controversies that reflected broader debates about accountability, institutional responsibility and inclusion in hockey. The Vegas Golden Knights’ signing of Carter Hart in 2025 drew criticism from some fans and media figures . Hart was one of the five former Hockey Canada players charged in an alleged 2018 sexual assault; all five were found not guilty in July 2025 . During the Stanley Cup Final, some fans chanted “no means no” when Hart was on the ice. The Edmonton Oilers’ later signing of another former Hockey Canada player who had been charged in the same case and was also found not guilty prompted longtime Oilers fan Mama Stanley to announce she would no longer support the team . The teams’ recent off-season hiring of Mike Babcock, who has been accused of abusive coaching tactics , was similarly controversial. Meanwhile, fans pushed back against the Dallas Stars’ announcement that it would not hold a Pride Night during the team’s 2026-27 season at a time when discussions about queerness and hockey were receiving increased attention. Challenging hockey culture The fact that these recent decisions are controversial suggests that a new generation of hockey fans have entered the arena. I am in the early phases of a research project about online hockey “counterpublics” with my colleague, creator culture expert Jess Rauchberg. A counterpublic is a group that has been excluded from the dominant discourse and challenges normative ideas . Some early findings show that hockey content creators are using online spaces to criticize aspects of hockey culture and challenge the behaviours and traditions documented by Westhead. Our preliminary analysis of comments on NHL teams’ Pride Night social media posts suggests that many old school fans are guarding the sport from these incursions. While many fans embrace Pride Nights as forms of inclusivity, others respond with slurs or argue Pride has no place in hockey. Sports are imbued with social and political values, often leading to what political scientist Jules Boykoff calls “sportwashing,” or using sports to deflect from political crises and normalize nationalism and human rights abuses. Given that hockey is so tied to Canadian national identity , challenges to hockey culture can be seen by some fans as challenges to their own identities. Can stories change hockey? The hockey shows of the 2020s imagine a world in which hockey can be better. In Heated Rivalry , the two best hockey players in the league are queer men — a challenge to masculine ideals about who belongs in elite sport. In Off Campus , main protagonist Hannah receives support from an NHL prospect when she discloses her rape by a hockey player. Shoresy presents a version of hockey where women not only have a place in a hockey team’s front office, but can be respected leaders, and Indigenous players and management personnel are equal to their white counterparts. Sudbury Blueberry Bulldogs team manager Sanguinet (played by Harlan Blayne Kytwayhat) stands behind bench during hockey game in Shoresy . (Bell Media) Rachel Reid, the author of the romance series from which Heated Rivalry was adapted, has said she set out to challenge the culture of the sport she loved . In the wake of the show’s massive success, some NHL players have said they would support a gay teammate . But recent developments show hockey culture is difficult to challenge. While popular media seems to be confronting some of the norms embedded in hockey culture, hockey itself appears resistant to change. My research into online hockey counterpublics and fan responses to Pride Night suggests that supporters and critics are both actively shaping the future meaning of the sport. Popular media is challenging some of hockey’s traditional norms, but whether those challenges lead to broader changes within hockey itself remains to be seen. Clementine Oberst does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: The Métis are one of the most misunderstood Indigenous groups in Canada . The Canadian Constitution recognizes that “Aboriginal peoples of Canada includes the Indian, Inuit and Métis Peoples of Canada,” yet in practical terms the Métis have continually fought, and continue to fight, to have their inherent rights as Indigenous people fully recognized. Our peoplehood comes from a shared history, political will, cultural traditions and kinship networks that predate colonial boundaries . Our homeland spans the Prairie provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba as well as parts of British Columbia, Ontario, the Northwest Territories and North Dakota. Yet we are often and erroneously mistaken as simply half European and half First Nation. As a post-contact people who were seen as different from our First Nations relatives by those who encountered us, we don’t fit easily into racial categories. Our positioning between worlds presents a conundrum for those from outside the Métis community as we proudly embrace our complexities, ambiguities and contradictions . Still, this complexity has caused confusion and left us vulnerable to those who knowingly exploit Canadians’ widespread lack of knowing. Read more: Becoming Indigenous: The rise of Eastern Métis in Canada Knowing this, there is a great need for ongoing authentic Métis voice and representation, and expression of our unique cultural identity. Seldom-heard Métis truths In these times of “Truths Before Reconciliation,” one of the lesser-known facts in Canadian history is that Métis people have routinely asserted their Indigeneity and rights through legal means . As respected Métis author and retired lawyer Jean Teillet details in The North-West Is Our Mother The Story of Louis Riel’s People, the Métis Nation (2021), the Métis have gathered and organized ever since the birth of our nation. These meetings included legal discussions and plans. Métis historian Lawrence Barkwell details some of the numerous petitions sent to the Dominion of Canada starting in the mid-1840s as the Métis made extensive use of their right to petition the government for recognition of their rights, including land rights. Very few, if any, of these petitions proved successful. Hopeful moments unrealized The inclusion of the Métis into the Canadian Constitution in 1982 as one of three “Aboriginal” groups was a promising moment led by Métis leader Harry Daniels and others. In the years that followed, another hopeful moment arrived with the Supreme Court of Canada’s Powley decision that asserted Indigenous harvesting rights for Métis people. But this court-imposed definition of the Métis, with its geographical and cultural limitations set out in “the 10-point Powley Test,” raised more questions than solutions . Years passed, and another moment of hope was sparked in 2016 with the Daniels decision from the Supreme Court of Canada that ruled Métis and non-status peoples fall under the category “Indians” under section 91(24) of the Constitution Act, 1867. However, the legal ruling’s “mixed ancestry” wording was problematic. Ultimately, myriad confusing legal decisions have stalled progress in Métis rights recognition — for example, in land rights, education and health. articles.content: A Canadian non-profit performance rights organization is suing Suno, an American genAI music creation platform, over streaming AI outputs that allegedly replicate songs without consent or compensation. The Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada (SOCAN) lawsuit cites 150 Suno songs that it says are identical or nearly identical to the works of Canadian artists including Joni Mitchell, The Weeknd, The Tragically Hip and others. SOCAN wants the AI company to comply with copyright law and for artists to have a say in how their works are used (or not). The statement of claim , which seeks $20,000 per work and $10,000,000 for infringement, joins a series of recent lawsuits against Suno. These include a US$500-million joint copyright lawsuit originally launched by major labels of Warner, Sony and Universal ( Warner has since signed a licensing deal with Suno ) and a class-action lawsuit from Jason Isbell and other musicians . There are also music publisher and record label lawsuits. SOCAN’s lawsuit raises questions about the place of Canadian artists in a music industry increasingly shaped by American tech companies. SOCAN’s complaint says in response to a prompt consisting of lyrics to ‘Both Sides Now’ by Joni Mitchell, Suno generated an output that is virtually identical including in melody, harmony and lyrics. (SUNO) Musician livelihoods at risk A wide range of issues pertaining to AI technology and musicmaking are putting musician livelihoods at risk. “It definitely feels like an existential struggle for artists today against AI,” rapper Cadence Weapon told The Canadian Press . The artist says 129 of his songs have been found in datasets to train AI music generators. We conducted a survey this past summer with 267 working musicians in Canada . The survey was sent to 1,025 musicians ( Polaris-longlisted artists between 2006-25 who have appeared on the Earshot charts seven or more times with Gold records; some were added for geographic representation). We asked 26 questions about their music-making and relationships to aspects of the music industry, including companies like Spotify, Live Nation and Suno. Read more: Artists’ Spotify criticisms point to larger ways musicians lose with streaming — here’s 3 changes to help in Canada Musician responses We found that 87 per cent of respondents view AI technology in music creation negatively. One respondent said they are “personally and professionally offended by the existence and use of genAI tools for artistic practices” and that the AI tech tools encourage the theft of copyrighted works. Another said AI tools are compromising musicians’ ability to make money from music. One artist said they avoid AI “like the plague.” The majority of survey responses indicate a clear line between creativity and the type of music production encouraged by a platform like Suno. These artist responses challenge the way Suno is marketed to users. A recent post by the company said that Suno is “ grateful to build tools that let everyone experience the joy of making music .” The survey also found many Canadian musicians feel forced into using particular tools or platforms, or forced to work with large companies that dominate within a particular sector of the music industry. In one survey response to a question asking about an artist’s relationship to ticketing company Ticketmaster and concert promoter Live Nation, the respondent said they are in “a relationship, but forced into it.” Proliferating AI-generated content AI music is becoming a battleground over the future of tech, culture and community. In January 2026, Billboard magazine reported on a media consumption survey that found the vast majority of music consumers in the United States are uninterested in engaging with AI-generated songs as well. Another U.S.-based survey documented increased discomfort with GenAI in music , especially among younger listeners. Part of this growing distaste for AI music comes from increased exposure. A recent example of this unwelcome intrusion happened when one of the authors of this story was listening to YouTube Music and was algorithmically recommended an AI song , which had a similar sound to the country-folk artist that was originally selected. The YouTuber whose profile is listed as posting this song is Lee Vybrony, who uses AI avatars of sexualized women to generate videos for a range of AI-generated songs and whose profile has more than 32,000 subscribers. One of Vybrony’s songs, “Both Sides of Us,” seems to rip off Joni Mitchell’s “Both Sides Now.” AI avatars front AI-generated songs, including one that appears to rip off Joni Mitchell’s ‘Both Sides Now.’ (YouTube) Trade, sovereignty concerns For Canadian musicians, artists and other creators the stakes are raised by the current trade war with the U.S. During the latest skirmish over tariffs, U.S. negotiators demanded Canada drop requirements for streamers like Netflix to promote Canadian content. But Canadian cultural production should not be sacrificed. If anything, the hostility toward our sovereignty and protecting our culture should be a call to strengthen these laws and support Canadian artists. Read more: Caught between culture and commerce: Canada’s high-stakes trade clash with the United States Artist input into copyright In addition to efforts by SOCAN and others to stop the exploitation and mining of artistic works, a broader range of solutions are needed if we are to ensure artist livelihoods are protected and celebrated. It’s important that artists influence policymaking, particularly copyright law . Read more: Should global media giants shape our cultural and media policy? Lessons from satellite radio AI-generated music needs to be labelled on streaming platforms . Listeners should be empowered to filter it out if they choose. Ideally, users should have to opt-in to AI-generated music. The Online Streaming Act should be expanded to require a certain percentage of Canadian content be heard, viewed and promoted across online and streaming platforms, just as Canadian content regulations have done for broadcast radio. Tighter regulation, more competition We also need to advocate for digital tools and platforms that are built and regulated in Canada , as well as more competition in the music industries. In the U.S., a jury recently decided Live Nation and Ticketmaster have operated as a monopoly and overcharged fans . Recently, the Consumers Council of Canada filed an application to sue Live Nation in Canada around similar concerns . And as we’ve documented , consolidation in the Canadian music industry by non-Canadian companies has only tightened: Universal, Warner and Sony have a triopoly in the recording and publishing market; SiriusXM has a monopoly in satellite radio and Google/YouTube, Spotify, Apple and Amazon have an oligopoly of the streaming music market. “Now old friends are acting strange,” Mitchell wrote back in 1967 , after she had relocated to the U.S. from Canada a couple of years prior . “Well something’s lost,” Mitchell laments, “but something’s gained.” Through strategic opposition to tech platforms and music monopolies, we could gain a music industry that allows Canadian music to flourish. articles.content: A still from Saffron Kingdom (Daffodil Studios) Saffron Kingdom is a rare and special film about Kashmir, created by a Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh. Although the film was released in 2024 (Daffodil Studios), there was only one Canadian screening, in October 2025 , meaning it was a hard film to see. That’s changed with its recent release on the streaming service Watermelon Plus, making the drama available to a larger audience. The film offers a rare glimpse into how everyday life in Kashmir is impacted under militarization and surveillance. The Indian state prefers to tell a different version of the story. The film is centred on Masrat, a woman from Indian-administered Kashmir who, after her husband’s enforced disappearance in 2014, escapes the valley with her son. The movie follows her family’s displacement over three generations from their life in Kashmir to their current life in Atlanta, Ga. The film uses memory and family stories to guide viewers through Kashmir’s political history. It emphasizes silence, rituals and inherited grief. It portrays displacement not as a clear timeline of dates and policies but as a complex loss transmitted across generations, often explained imperfectly. Read more: Borders and orders: How settler-government occupations violate Kashmiri sovereignty The filmmaker’s father, well-known Kashmiri singer Ghulam Nabi Sheikh , disappeared in 2003 while travelling by train. His family describe it as an enforced disappearance by the Indian army. Though the film is not autobiographical, it’s inspired by true events as it deals with the collective issue of disappearance, including extrajudicial killings, and political repression in Kashmir . Sheikh says the film grew out of his years spent travelling throughout Kashmir and hearing stories of loss and violence. The trailer for Saffron Kingdom (Daffodil Studios). Reclaiming the story of Kashmir The film opens in Jammu and Kashmir’s summer capital of Srinagar in 1989. Young Masrat lives a simple life. Her father is teaching her to nurture their land. But her childhood is disrupted when the Indian military suddenly barges in and the child, threatened, runs into the arms of her aunt. The army attacks her father, a revolutionary poet. The film portrays the Gowkadal massacre of January 1991 through the story of Masrat’s family. On the day of her paternal aunt’s wedding, the aunt’s fiancé is killed in the massacre and the Indian army kills Masrat’s father at the wedding. For most of its cinematic history, India has largely controlled Kashmir’s story, spending years turning the area into a national fantasy and using it as a setting for romance, honeymoon songs and beautiful landscapes. It’s a narrative that has helped sustain Kashmir’s image as a tourist destination. In her book Territory of Desire: Representing the Valley of Kashmir , Prof. Ananya Jahanara Kabir of King’s College London explains how Bollywood has leaned heavily on propaganda. More recently, Kashmir has been serving as a backdrop for stories about the Indian military. In both portrayals, Kashmiris are generally in the background, either as props or villains. For many years, external voices have predominantly shaped the global and Indian narratives of Kashmir’s history. In contrast, Saffron Kingdom focuses not on Kashmir as the Indian state views it, but on the local perspective. It’s about a Kashmiri family and an honest portrayal of the very real impact the conflict has had on their lives. Why the film couldn’t be made in Kashmir A viewer may note the absence of genuine Kashmiri locations and actors. In fact, some critics note that the film’s English-accented dialogue and largely non-Kashmiri cast creates distance from the subject. However, this is not due to artistic choices or financial limits. Sheikh explained in interviews why Saffron Kingdom could not be filmed in Kashmir and why none of the Kashmiri characters are played by people living there. He said it would be impossible to make the film under current circumstances and warned that families of local actors likely would have faced retaliation from Indian security forces. Press freedom has declined sharply since 2019. In the years following the abrogation of Article 370 , an article of the Indian Constitution that granted some autonomy to Jammu and Kashmir — including the right to have their own constitution and some legal and land rights — press freedom has declined. Read more: In India, Modi’s nationalism quashes dissent with help from the media Journalists are faced with increased surveillance , harassment, travel restrictions and legal action under anti-terror laws because of their reporting. By streaming Arfat Sheikh’s Saffron Kingdom , Watermelon Plus is providing a rare platform for Kashmiri stories told by Kashmiris. The film may help to bring international attention to Kashmir’s overlooked suffering. The film ends with an interview with the last survivor of the Gowkadal massacre. Saffron Kingdom is available to view on Watermelon Plus. Shambhavi Siddhi does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

Why the film couldn’t be made in Kashmir A viewer may note the absence of genuine Kashmiri locations and actors. In fact, some critics note that the film’s English-accented dialogue and largely non-Kashmiri cast creates distance from the subject. However, this is not due to artistic choices or financial limits. Sheikh explained in interviews why Saffron Kingdom could not be filmed in Kashmir and why none of the Kashmiri characters are played by people living there. He said it would be impossible to make the film under current circumstances and warned that families of local actors likely would have faced retaliation from Indian security forces. Press freedom has declined sharply since 2019. In the years following the abrogation of Article 370 , an article of the Indian Constitution that granted some autonomy to Jammu and Kashmir — including the right to have their own constitution and some legal and land rights — press freedom has declined. By streaming Arfat Sheikh’s Saffron Kingdom , Watermelon Plus is providing a rare platform for Kashmiri stories told by Kashmiris. The film may help to bring international attention to Kashmir’s overlooked suffering. The film ends with an interview with the last survivor of the Gowkadal massacre. articles.content: Behavioural scientist Louis Busch weaves Indigenous teachings from Knowledge Keepers across Turtle Island with western psychological practice. Busch, a Bear Clan member of Nisichawayasihk Cree Nation, offers a framework for moving through pain rather than around it. In this Q&A, the psychotherapist talks about his book, Carry Your Heart: Indigenous Helping Wisdom and the Science of Psychological Flexibility , that integrates these two ways of knowing. The Conversation Canada: What does it mean to “carry your heart” in life? Louis Busch: That teaching came from a relative of mine. The Cree word is kita-pimōtātamān kitēb . It loosely translates to “walking while carrying your heart.” In a practical sense, it means noticing the urge to flee from our difficult experiences, whether a worry, a bad memory, grief, a difficult experience or an intrusive thought. Often, we are very motivated to find a distraction, a positive affirmation, medication — whatever we can get relief from. And that’s normal, but I think to “carry your heart” means to pause, look at [the difficult experiences], and then hold them in a gentle way and make a bit of space for them. [While working on this book], I really loved seeing the synergies of some of these First Nations teachings and the things that I had learned in acceptance and commitment therapy . We’ve been trained from Day One [that] the pursuit of happiness is the ultimate goal of being alive. And if you’re not doing that, there’s something wrong with you, right? You are broken. You’re pathological. You have some kind of dysfunction, and it’s inside you. It’s this thing that you have. So to ask somebody to do something different, it’s like flipping the idea of healing on its head. TCC: You organize the book around belonging through kinship, presence and purposeful action. Can you talk about structure? LB: At first I thought I was going to write a clinical manual, a “how to work with First Nations Peoples in a culturally safe way.” That was my goal initially. I thought it was important to have a strong first section on positionality — who am I and why am I writing this. Then I started getting into typical textbook on culturally adapted therapies. I started to lose motivation a bit, and I shared it with a friend of mine. She said, “I was hooked, then when I got to the second chapter, I thought, ‘Where did you go?’” I thought a lot about [that]: if [I wrote that kind of] book, I would probably talk about the people I learned from and the people who I think have really guided me on this journey. So the book’s structure [turned into] a bit of a road trip of healing and learning — visiting with [Elders], and then pausing to reflect on my own experience with whatever they were sharing. I was able to [include] some important messages about how we do healing in the colonial system that exists around us. I decided to break the book down to three core teachings. It shouldn’t be viewed as “here is the wisdom of the Indigenous Peoples of Canada or North America,” instead it should be looked at as “here is the wisdom of these particular Knowledge Keepers, and their context Nations, in dialogue with me.” And hopefully that’ll be useful for you. But it certainly does not reflect an Indigenous philosophy on wellness or an Indigenous therapy. We’re 600-plus nations in Canada, 80-plus language families, all different experiences and languages and spirituality and protocols. I talked to lots of different people because I feel like there are just such rich experiences, but I hope people walk away knowing that the book is limited to those relationships and contexts. TCC: Indigenous knowledge has a long history of being extracted and repackaged by non-Indigenous institutions for profit. How did you think about this tension when writing for a mainstream publisher? LB: It was a very hard book to write because that thought was always in my mind: how do I protect our communities, how do I protect this knowledge and how do I share it in a way that is respectful but also may benefit people? Though I primarily wrote it for Indigenous Peoples, when we say all our relations, we mean everybody in the world. We’re all relatives. I say this is for you if you are struggling with your experiences. Just please, treat it respectfully as you would treat your own grandmother’s teachings. There are different forms or levels of knowledge. There is sacred knowledge, and there is community knowledge, and some of those things are not meant to be shared in the pages of a book. Like a description of a ceremony in great detail or specific stories that we only share at specific times and with specific people. So [certain elements] fit within the realm of sacred knowledge, and maybe should be protected or at least communicated in a way that the Knowledge Keepers are comfortable with. What I [would tell] the reader is that if you are interested in this particular thing that I’m not going to talk about, take some tobacco, find a Knowledge Keeper and ask the question — do it in a respectful way. I had quite a bit of discomfort with the idea of taking the teachings of Elders and Knowledge Keepers and putting them out in a market. Books sell. So one of the ways that I have approached that is that the author royalties that come after the publication of the book will go to the Thunderbird Partnership Foundation and the Legacy of Hope Foundation . Anything that comes from this book, at least financially, goes right back into community. And that makes me feel a bit better about it. The Elders were happy with that also. articles.content: Rocky Horror fans everywhere have been celebrating the life and work of actor and cult cinema icon Tim Curry, who passed away at the age of 80 at his home in Los Angeles . Curry brought distinctive charisma, energy and dramatic flair to countless films, including Annie (1982), Clue (1985), Legend (1985) and Home Alone 2: Lost in New York (1992). Children of the 1990s may remember him as the murderous, wisecracking clown Pennywise in the TV adaptation of Stephen King’s It (1990) . Curry was also a familiar face on Broadway and London’s West End, where he starred in many productions, including Amadeus (1979) and Spamalot (2005). An illustrious, nearly six-decade career notwithstanding, Curry remained best known for his 1975 screen debut as The Rocky Horror Picture Show ’s Dr. Frank-N-Furter, the mischievous, magnetic, stiletto- and corset-clad mad scientist who seduces the straight-laced Brad and Janet (Barry Bostwick and Susan Sarandon) on a fateful, stormy night. This is the image that Curry’s name has always conjured for me. Like several generations before me, singing along to Dr. Frank-N-Furter’s “Sweet Transvestite” at midnight Rocky Horror screenings has been somewhat of a tradition. Rocky Horror would also come to have a greater impact on my academic and professional life later on. Yet reflecting on the broader strokes of Curry’s career after news of his passing, I am reminded of the significance that even his lesser-known roles had played in my own life. The many faces of Tim Curry Kids are often captivated by Dickensian-style orphan tales, an obsession Annie cemented for me early on. Witches and magic were another fixation, and I’d direct anyone looking for a hit of ‘80s nostalgia to Curry’s musical number as The Grand Wizard in The Worst Witch (1986). These are the performances I connected to most. But reading through Curry’s extensive resumé, it would be difficult to overstate the number of “Oh, that was him too?” exclamations that occurred along the way. Curry voiced several cartoons I watched regularly, including FernGully: The Last Rainforest (1992) and The Wild Thornberrys (1998–2004) . He playfully satirized his Rocky Horror fame in the raunchy horror parody Scary Movie 2 (2001) , a clandestine viewing at my seventh-grade sleepover, and helped me pass the time at a babysitting gig or two in Clue and Home Alone 2: Lost in New York . A compilation of Tim Curry’s performances from WatchMojo. My inability to recognize Curry in some of these performances initially is not to imply that he was unmemorable. Rather, it speaks to his ability to immerse himself and disappear fully into his roles. I have little memory of Tim Curry the actor — or the person — growing up. But I do know that It ’s Pennywise terrified me, and I remember cheering as orphan Annie outwitted the schemes of Curry’s villainous Rooster Hannigan. The art of disappearing Curry himself aspired toward this status of absolute absorption for his characters. In his 2025 memoir Vagabond Curry wrote admiringly of fellow actor Alec Guinness, who prepared for roles by walking down busy streets in character with the goal of not being recognized. For Curry, acting was a way of disappearing or of hiding in plain sight. It might have been a contradictory state of being, but Curry, fittingly, saw contradiction as one of the most integral and fascinating aspects of human nature. Acting was a vehicle for exploring such contradictions; a way to understand the most paradoxical aspects of human emotion, as Curry suggested in his memoir: “Professionally, the lure of pursuing contradictions has drawn me toward complex characters or compelled me to make them more complex and nuanced.” 'Making the darkness sparkle’ Curry often played villains and antagonists: malicious characters who, on the surface, are difficult to root for, yet remain beguiling and charismatic. He intentionally infused a level of playfulness into even his most nefarious roles, a process he referred to as “mak[ing] the darkness sparkle.” His empathetic desire to explore even his most unlikable characters can be traced back to the most complex and challenging aspects of his own early life. Growing up modestly in the “dull, strange time” of post-Second World War England, Curry and his older sister Judy lost their father when he was 11 or 12. Curry described his mother as both emotionally distant and highly mercurial, traits that he, retrospectively, attributed to his mother’s own childhood neglect. In his memoir, Curry does not shy away from the pain these early experiences caused him, writing with a level of humility and vulnerability that lends an even greater depth to his surviving work. He also credits some of his key performance techniques to his mother. Her frequent, irate, outbursts became an acting masterclass emotional expression — experiences he would later draw on in his performances. From church choirs to Rocky Horror In his memoir, Curry reflects on his youth and early career, describing himself as an imaginative and unusual child who discovered his love for singing and performance through church choirs. While away at boarding school, acting became a satisfying and intellectually stimulating reprieve from what was often a lonely and isolating experience. Curry also recounts his time studying theatre and literature at the University of Birmingham and his eventual emergence onto the London theatre scene. Success did not always come easily, and he often took a scrappy, hardscrabble approach. One of his most memorable stories concerns his first major audition for the original London stage production of Hair . Curry recounts that, lacking the required credentials and experience, he lied about both . By the time the truth came out, he had already charmed the casting directors with his musical rendition of “Cool” from West Side Story . Connections made with Rocky Horror creator Richard O’Brien during the production of Hair would eventually lead to Curry’s casting in the ground-breaking 1973 London stage production . The creative flair and unmistakably campy, queer-coded sex appeal that Curry brought to the Frank-N-Furter role ensured that director Jim Sharman considered no other actor sufficient for the 1975 film adaptation , even as stars like Mick Jagger vied for the part. The Rocky Horror Picture Show is still among the most screened titles worldwide, and Curry’s central performance has undoubtedly been integral to its enduring popularity and definitive cult status. With his powerful voice and electric presence, there is little danger of Curry fading into obscurity. He continues to strut across midnight movie screens everywhere, adding a much-needed “sparkle” to the darkness.
